utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Hedaraly, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can at the outset invite you once again to try to pause between my question and your answer in order to assist me in not speaking too quickly. We left off yesterday discussing page 40 of your report and specifically the order assigning Mr. Jonjic, the order issued by General Cermak. Do you remember that discussion?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, I wanted to move to the next paragraph in your report, which is a paragraph starting at line 28, where you discuss other similar issues. First you refer to D761, which is an order from General Cermak to temporarily assign seven members of the 142nd Home Guards Regiment to the Knin garrison on 11 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And maybe we could have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in the meantime let me -- in your report at lines 33 and 34, you state that: "There appeared to be no response to the order." General, if this was an order from General Cermak assigning people to the Knin garrison, why would there be a response?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for some evidence that those soldiers had actually turned up and done what they were supposed to do, and I saw none of it. I might have expected to see some further correspondence as you will see later in the next exhibit, which you might be showing me, concerning their sort of welfare, their pay, their -- their overall administration. I didn't see any of that, and, therefore, I question whether that order was ever -- whether that order actually took place, whether those soldiers turned up. Because I have to say what you know I'm going to say, he had no authority to order those men to be attached to his -- his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you also know we disagree on -- on that. But going back to your answer, you said that you were looking for some evidence that those soldiers had actually turned up and done what they were supposed to do. Now, with the exception of the two documents that you refer to later on, did you see any other evidence that this -- these soldiers did not turn up?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no evidence they did not turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, which is D762, which is ten days later, 21st of August. And this is a request from General Cermak to General Gotovina for 65 conscripts, and then we have the response reference in your letter from General Gotovina. Now at this time in the order that will come up shortly, which is D762, this time General Cermak asks for 65 conscripts and does not identify any specific ones. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So in this sense, this request is different from the previous order in that it doesn't say, "I order A, B, and C, specifically," but rather says, "I asked for 65 men. Please send them to me."

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Then we have the response from General Gotovina which is D764, where in fact General Gotovina formally subordinates 147 members, the entire 3rd company or the third battalion - I get those confused with the 3rd of the 3rd of the 142nd Regiment. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just to go back to the conversation we had yesterday, these 147 soldiers would then be fully subordinated to General Cermak, not only for matters of order and discipline, correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- can I just address -- it looks as if that is true. No, not quite true. I'm sorry, I missed the line. Paragraph 2 says: "The commander of the 142nd Home Guard Regiment will keep on the payroll the soldiers from the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion. So the commander, General Gotovina, has authorised the commanding officer of that regiment to maintain administrative control, in terms of the payroll. So there is not a complete subordination. It is what I would term limited subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But this subordination would extent to any other non-administrative task. This is the only limitation, this administrative one.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So, in that sense, it goes beyond just order and discipline; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He has a right to task them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And there is nothing that you have seen either in the request from General Cermak or the order from General Gotovina which suggests that the previous order regarding those seven individuals was not implemented ten days earlier.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's true. There was no evidence either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to move now to the UNCRO vehicles orders, and I know we have seen those yesterday, so the Chamber is very familiar with them. So I will try to deal with the matter as efficiently as possible. And you discuss in your report, General Cermak's authority to issue orders generally, and you refer to a number of these order, D788, D303, D503. And I think we discussed yesterday, or if we did not, I -- I suspect you will agree with me that at least those documents look like orders. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they have "order" written on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And they also say that they should come into effect immediately.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And as we discussed yesterday, if we accept your position that General Cermak did not have that authority, he was acting as if he did or at least he thought he had the authority; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the way he wrote it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just to summarise briefly the orders relating to the UNCRO vehicles, and I'm just doing this in the interests of time, and if I -- if I don't summarise accurately, please let me know. So General Cermak issued orders, D303 and D503, that he didn't have the authority to issue. Then he subsequently made a request to General Gotovina, D304, and that following that request, General Gotovina issued an order, D305; and that showed you that General Cermak was beginning to understand the chain of command and the principles of subordination. That's on page 42 and 43 of your report. Have I summarized accurately your position?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's start with D303 which is an order from the 9 August to the military police and the civilian police to set up teams to find these specific UN vehicles. Right, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I have seen that one. It's in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then the next one is D503, which, this time, is an order from the 12th of August to the military police and the civilian police to set up teams to find a total of 12 vehicles, if in counted them properly, or in that area. You can wait for it to come up, but if you remember --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So the recipient of this order are the military police and the civilian police; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the order that is given to them, accepting our difference of opinion on Mr. Cermak's authority, the order given to them is to set up teams to find the vehicles; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, on the same day as this order, General Cermak sends a request to General Gotovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have D304. If we can just scroll down so the witness can see the complete first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if -- can I move to the next page, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me that what General Cermak is requesting is not for General Gotovina to send an order to the military police but, rather, asking General Gotovina to inform the HV unit commanders of the Split Military District of the need to urgently return the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just to be clear, General Gotovina is the commander of the Split Military District. He is General Cermak's immediate superior as the garrison commander, correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the regulations, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is therefore normal that he would send a request rather than an order?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Cermak would request assistance from General Gotovina, that is the correct way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now the resulting order from General Gotovina the next day, D305, and in this order General Gotovina orders the commanders of all the units of the Split Military District to return the vehicles; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to the seconds page in the English, we can see the list of all the units under General Gotovina's command; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one clarification. I'm sure this is just an oversight by my learned friend. But the request, I believe, that is in 304, D304, is sent to the Chief of Staff of the Split Military District and not to General Gotovina. So just for clarity in the record, I think that that's accurate, is it not, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'll look at, but I will take your [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, General, just to go back to this order on the screen. General Gotovina had the authority to issue this order; correct? To his own units.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, General, you will agree with me that the orders issued by General Cermak were quite of a different nature than the one issued here by General Gotovina. General Cermak ordered the military police and the civilian police - and I know I you dispute his authority to do so - but he ordered the military police and the civilian police to form teams and find the vehicles, whereas General Gotovina issued orders to his unit commanders to return those vehicles. Now, those are two very different types of orders. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So in your report, when you are conflating the two and suggesting that General Cermak realised he could not issue an order and that he then asked General Gotovina to issue it for him once he began to, as you say, understand the chain of command and the principles of subordination, based on these documents we've just seen that's not entirely correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, we're -- we -- we go round this circle of our different views. The first point I would want to make is that the simple writing of an order does not demonstrate you have the authority to write it. Secondly, General Gotovina was absolutely correct in producing an order, because he had the command, he exercises the command of all those units that we're looking at now and therefore has the responsibility to ensure that military discipline, good order and military discipline is -- is properly -- properly carried out. What General Cermak was doing, I have suggested, is that he was learning that if he wanted assistance from General Gotovina, then -- or if he wanted assistance to his headquarters, whether that be manpower or whatever else, then the proper thing to do was to request that, that is, in the way that a subordinate commander does. The orders he wrote to -- the so-called orders he wrote to the police for which he had no authority, as I have said and we will continue to disagree about that, I'm sure, where in fact in response to demands from the United Nations, from UNCRO, from commander Sector South, and you will know there was a series of meetings in which commander Sector South expressed his concern about this. At this stage, General Cermak had been in place - I'm just looking at my notes - three days, two days, the 8th of August. You will recall that I've said on many occasions he was a man who was given no preparation time, who came from a completely different background, a commercial background and a political background, who, I think, and my judgement is, that you see here him attempting to meet the demands that were being imposed upon him by the United Nations. He did it in the best way possible. Could you argue, though I doubt if he knew that he had a coordinating and cooperating requirement in the garrison orders, because I doubt if he'd actually read them by that time. He might have done, but I question whether he would have done. But that is another issue. You could see this as part of his coordination and cooperation responsibility, that actually this -- that order - and it should not a have been written as an order, I would absolutely agree; it would be much better if he hadn't done it - may have been the subject of coordination that had already been done between the police and -- and his headquarters. I have no evidence of that. That is a deduction that you could make, based upon the -- the instructions that are there that a garrison commander will carry out these coordination and cooperation functions. That is a rather long answer to your question, but I'm afraid that I -- I fear that you're trying to simplify and chop things up into packages and take it outside the overall context. I go back to my original point: That he no authority to wrote those orders. We will disagree about that, and it will be for the Chamber to decide who they -- who they believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sir, my question was limited to those three or four orders, because you have presented them in your report as suggesting something, as suggesting that, after the first order, which is -- after one of the orders, which is the 11th of August, General Cermak learned the principles of subordination and then asked General Gotovina to issue the order for him. And that -- this specific question was not about the whole authority of General Cermak or the military police. It was based on your report, your conclusions, based on those documents, those specific documents, and what I'm telling you, what I'm suggesting to you is that those three documents that have you cited in that paragraph of your report do not actually support your conclusion in that paragraph of your report.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not ask, actually, General Gotovina to write the order for him. He was not in a position to dictate what order General Gotovina gave. He requested, first of all, for manpower. It was up to General Gotovina to decide whether to give him any manpower and for them to -- for -- then for him to allocate that manpower and give the order to those soldiers that were properly subordinated to General Gotovina, that they should be resubordinated for a specific task and for a specific time, although that was not clear, to General Cermak. The second was requesting that General Gotovina should use the -- his chain of command in a disciplinary sense to remind his commanders that it was wrong to steal vehicles, and if they had them they should hand them back. So on neither occasion did -- I would suggest did General Cermak ask General Gotovina to write an order for him. He merely presented General Gotovina with two decisions to make. One was, was he going provide the manpower? Secondly, was he going to write this letter to the chain of command? And it is a chain of command responsibility. If I may, just make one other comment. We have tended to paint discipline in a geographical sense. Primarily, the application of military discipline is to do with subordination. It doesn't matter where those soldiers might be geographically. They remain under the command of their superior commander. We have tended to allow ourselves, I believe, to -- to paint discipline as a geographical issue within the garrison area. But I make that as a general point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I know there is a lot of issues that we cover, but if you could try to focus on my questions. I do understand, and I have not interrupted you all day yesterday or today when the answers were quite long. But if you would please try to focus on the question.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for digressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's then turn to the issue of the military police, which you discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Kehoe, you earlier said you were kind enough to assist Mr. Hedaraly into whom the D304 was addressed, and you said it was addressed to the Chief of Staff. It is actually addressed to the Military District Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Attention Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you added something, that it was not addressed to General Gotovina. To some extent, that may be right. That is that he was not the person mentioned there. At the same time you can't say that General Gotovina was not covered, by a rather general expression, Military District Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, obviously the next day General Gotovina issued the order which is D305. So his Chief of Staff made him aware of it. But just in the spirit of moving these documents through, clearly, the intent in this request in D304 was that it come to the attention or being sent to then General Ademi. So it was just in the spirit of clarity on this issue. And if you -- on this particular order which is D3305.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking to start this whole discussion again. But the most precise correction would have been that it was not addressed General Gotovina, instead it was addressed to the Military District Command, attention Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I stand corrected if I was inaccurate in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In page 20 of your report, there is an organigram that is reproduced there. There is also a colour version that perhaps may assist everyone if we pull it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 2D00786.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, did you prepare this organigram yourself?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you review the sources on the right, or did you just accept this as an accurate depiction of the command relationship between what you call the operational formation and units and the military police?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw nothing when I was reading the sources on the right, which led me to question the accuracy of that -- that diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go at the bottom of the page, completely at the bottom, there is a -- on top of the name there is a -- the number there is a reference to Zeljko Basic, subordination, 9, 2008. Can you tell the Court what that is or who Zeljko Basic is, or do you have any information for us?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Zeljko Basic is somebody who works in the Cermak Defence team. I would stand to be corrected, if I've got the name wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sure you would be if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Silence was a good sign there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you can go back a little towards the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In the box "command relationship," here you have also the words "effective control" discussed. I think we briefly touched on that yesterday. I understand you when you use effective control in this sense, or, rather, you adopted this diagram. You did not refer to the legal or technical aspects of effective control under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And based on that organigram, you stated at the bottom of page 20, line 6: "The only relationship shown between the military police and garrison headquarters is through the HQ of the Military District, which itself, has a cooperation and coordination relationship with the appropriate military police unit." So if we can just scroll down a little bit, there is no, you state, from this organigram, no direct link between garrison command and any relationship with the military police, except through the Military District. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Please look at it.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just scroll down once again just to remind myself of the colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Scroll down, please. Yeah. Yes, thank you. Thank you, I'm happy to say that I could see no formal linkage between garrison commanders and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go to D -- sorry, D34, which I know you are familiar with because you have cited it in your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, am I right or wrong that in the black and white copy the reference to Zeljko Basic is -- at least does not appear in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You are absolutely correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, although we are supposed to look at a colour version of a document, it gives more than just the colour version. It gives subordination, Zeljko Basic subordination, 9, 2008 which does not appear in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Mr. President. You're absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could ask the witness what, apart from that, he thinks that Mr. Zeljko Basic is someone who works in the Cermak Defence team, whether he -- what does "subordination 9, 2008" mean as far as you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely -- no idea, Your Honour. I have not idea what that means. To be honest, I hadn't even actually noticed it on the coloured copy. I looked down at that bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now who put the -- the picture in black and white into the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I put it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I -- I didn't check that it was a complete coverage. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you were a computer illiterate from what I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you were able to put this document in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a certain amount of guidance from the help box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The help box, but it takes quite a bit to take out the reference to the Zeljko Basic who guided you in that, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody. I mean, there was no guidance to take out the Zeljko Basic. I didn't even know it was in there, and I have no idea why, whether I -- when I, actually, sort of focussed on it, whether I left it off, I have no idea. But I was not aware, as I said, to Mr. Hedaraly, I was not aware that that name was even on the bottom. I had not looked at that particular part. I was not conscious of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see that. But I'm trying to understand the mechanism through which the colour version finally ended up as a black and white version in the -- in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I think I -- I've squared off, as it were, to copy it on to my document, in order to put it in, and I guess I missed off that bottom piece. But as is -- as has been identified, there would have been little point in me trying to do that because it would have been exposed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let's follow up on Mr. President's question, but let's start with this document. We have it on the screen. And you are obviously familiar with this, correct, you've cited it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you have cited particularly the second page of this document to support your interpretation of the authority or, in your view, the limits on the authority of the garrison commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next page, the third page of the document in English; I believe the second one in the B/C/S. Did you also review these instructions in this document, or did you just focus on the first two pages, the organisational order?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I looked at those -- I looked at those instructions in a certain amount of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please, instruction number 4, which is titled: Employing military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it says: "The garrison commander is required to arrange a procedure with the closest unit of the military police of calling military police units and having them intervene in the case of unrest, accidents, et cetera, when a military police unit is indispensable to establish order and discipline in the area of the garrison. Also, arrange for the temporary employment of military police patrols to supervise work, discipline, and conduct of military personnel in public places." General, will you agree with me that this instruction relates to a direct relationship between the garrison command and the military police without going through the Military District, as we had it in the organigram?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber why in all your discussion about the relationship between garrison command and the military police you did not once refer to these instructions.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this talks about a procedure. These -- these regulations are written with peacetime in mind, not in a situation of -- of internal conflict, of a very complex nature. And from -- from my point of view, this is perfectly normal because this actually -- this reflects the requirement imposed upon the garrison commander to cooperate and coordinate, which we've seen and actually comes in paragraph 5 as well. Now, arranging a procedure is a process. It's an administrative process, to enable the military police to be used in their daily tasks, their regular daily tasks, which are all about good order and military discipline. And I didn't put it in because I felt that I had made the point that I wanted to make there, and indeed it comes out later where I talk about the contentions between the garrison headquarters and the military police in several parts of the report. But I think that is very important, that one understands that these are procedures. It's temporary employment. This does not give or -- and I don't believe it implies any authority of the ZM commander to be able to order the military police to conduct any form of operation. It is completely focussing on an administrative procedure, in line with his -- those orders and other instructions about coordination and cooperation with other agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand your answer. My question did not say that this gave the garrison commander authority to order. I simply said this illustrate a direct relationship when in your report you said there were no such direct relationships.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say in that there's no direct relationship, and I -- I question whether -- whether the word "direct relationship" I'm -- you will understand that I'm concerned that phrases like "direct relationship" could be taken to mean something else. I'm very keen that we understand precisely what we're talking about, as I know you are, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in that vein, all I am trying to point out is that I understand your reservations about direct relationship. But all I'm pointing out is that there is nothing in this instruction, in that number 4, about going through the Military District.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can we go back to the organigram, please, which was 65 ter 2D00786. And while it comes up, Mr. President, since it has been discussed in court and specific references to differences with the report, I think it makes sense to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just make one point which have I noticed in the terminology that is being used, and I think the witness has expressed his reservations. This is a diagram which you can see says subordination --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, just let me finish -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Cayley, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- if this proper in front of the witness, I'm just cautioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it's perfectly proper because I think the witness can see what it says. But the point I'm make is this: This a diagram about subordination. It says it very clearly. Mr. Hedaraly is using these words "direct relationship" to try and sort of get around this word subordination, and I think he should just be clear with the witness, because the witness has already made the point that is he concerned about using that phraseology. That's the point I'm making. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that be an objection to having admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't object to it being admitted, Your Honour. But what I just request is that the terminology that's being used with the witness is clear, so that there is no confusion in the transcript what the witness is actually talking about. Because we know that subordination, I think you will understand, has a very specific meaning and relationship has a rather ambiguous kind of meaning. That's the point that I'm making. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't dictate Mr. Hedaraly to phrase his questions in the way I or you would like to do that. At the same time, I think the witness has been very clear where he has expressed his concerns in the use of certain terminology and he explained what he means. Therefore, I would say the -- the warning signs are there, and if would you like to further elaborate on this in re-examination, of course, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2658.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2658 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just for my learned friend's reference, in page 20 of the witness's expert report, he says: "The only relationship shown between the military police and garrison headquarters is through the headquarters of the Military District."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are not, at this moment arguing the matter. We are using the time of the witness to hear his answers to questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, you testified yesterday that you have assisted -- you were present when Mr. Feldi testified; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present for part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that you had reviewed Mr. Feldi's report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reviewed Mr. Feldi's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you provide any assistance to the Cermak Defence team for the examination and re-examination of Mr. Feldi?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can ask Mr. Registrar to keep this exhibit on the screen, and if we can pull up next to it, D1673, which is the expert report of Mr. Feldi. And if we can just pick the English for now so we have the same language. And if we go to page 19 of that -- if we could have the two side by side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, General, were you present in court when -- when Mr. Feldi said that he drew most of the diagrams himself sometime back and then received them later on in an electronic format?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall hearing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. So the diagram on the right side of the screen that we see is -- was prepared by Mr. Feldi and was included in his expert report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you agree with me that there are some striking similarities between the diagram in your report and the diagram in Mr. Feldi's report; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you can further see that there a relationship of cooperation and coordination in Mr. Feldi's report between the garrison command and the military police which is absent in your report.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So if Mr. Feldi is correct, then that would also show that it was not the only relationship - as you used in your report, that word - between the garrison command and the military police, was through the Military District; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to talk more about this relationship, but I want to thank the Registrar for his assistance. And we have seen and discussed a few orders from General Cermak, the military police, both with respect to freedom of movement and the UNCRO -- UNCRO vehicles. Let me show you P973. And you will recall there are exchanges of letters on 10th and 11th of August between General Forand and General Cermak regarding freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: This here, what I'm going to show you is now, is the log-book of the duty officer of the 4th Company, Sibenik, 72nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to the entry for the 11th of August, which is page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You see the 11 August -- we'll wait for it in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it on my left-hand screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can ask the Registrar to find the right page in the B/C/S. I thought I had written it down, but apparently not. The entry of the 11th of August. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page in the English, there is an entry at 1150 stating: "The 72nd Military Police Battalion duty officer informed regarding a command of General Cermak that members of UNCRO have complete freedom of movement." So the duty officer recorded General Cermak's order as a command in his log-book. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you see this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I -- I had heard that such documents existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But you had never seen --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't personally looked at that, no. I had not seen that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was not part the bundle provided to you regarding the military police?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will clarify that. I knew such documents as in police log-books existed. But I had not seen that particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Does that mean that that was not provided in the bundle of documents relating to the military that Mr. Cayley provided to you in March --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I may be that I never actually saw it. I never, myself, looked at because it was Sibenik and I may have decided that it was not applicable. Correctly or incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So it was either not provided to you, or it may have been provided to you but you didn't review it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show you P1147, which is a letter from General Cermak to Mr. Philippe Augarde, which was the head of the ECMM mission at the time. And you can see in the second paragraph: "I sincerely regret the cited impermissible behaviour by a person in the uniform of a Croatian soldiers [sic]. I have issued an order to the MP to investigate the case and make every attempt to discover the perpetrator." Had you seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you've also seen other documents where General Cermak tells internationals that he has ordered an investigation --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- or has ordered, in fact, the military police to do things?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And these documents are not referenced in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you -- General Cermak was issuing orders. He expected them to be followed. In some cases, the recipient of them recorded them as an order. And he is also telling people -- it says "issuing orders." General, does that not indicate to you that, if we accept your view that General Cermak did not have the formal authority to issue these orders, it appeared as if he did have that authority?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- of course, it appears. I would be foolish to try and paint a picture that General Cermak did not impress some people with his apparent authority. I mean, he was a General. He was sent there as we discussed yesterday; he was sent there by the President. We all know that General Cermak was a successful businessman. He would have had -- he has a personality. He is a successful man, therefore he will have influenced people. I go back to my original comment that here is a man who was put into this post which he didn't understand. He thought his -- his -- his real task was the urban regeneration of Knin. He was there to help the Canadians but that developed into a much more profound and significant task of a point of contact. And I believe that General Cermak did what many people would do and took on to himself responsibilities which actually he didn't have. And did he that for the best possible motives, because he wished to be helpful. And there is evidence, as we know from General Leslie who says that General Cermak was a very helpful and cooperative person, as General Brigadier Forand says. So my argument is really that these have got to be taken in that context and not looked at in a very narrow legalistic way. I know that is the way the court -- I'm making a presumption, Your Honour, if I may. I know that is the way the Court may wish to do it or the Prosecution may wish to do it. But I hope you understand my concern is that we look at this wholistically as far as we possibly can. So we understand what was behind this apparent issuing -- this actual issuing of orders and the apparent belief that he the authority to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm also happy to report that we're doing much better with the interpreters today, General.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm learning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want do stay on this topic of the military police but talk about some of the answers that gave yesterday, both to Mr. Cayley and to Mr. Kehoe. And a the outset I just want to confirm what you stated yesterday, that you were not sure that you were provided the testimony of General Lausic but that, in any event you did not rely on it in any significant manner in coming to your conclusion. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I added that I looked at lot of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may not have done, but I did. As a matter of clarity, I looked at a lot of his documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that's clear from your report --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- obviously. And the same true for Mr. Dzolic, correct, you may not have reviewed his testimony but --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And also Mr. Simic would be the same?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that's why they are not referenced in the footnotes because those were not the documents that you relied on mainly?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that, in respect of the military police, your report is primarily based on the regulations and the documents you reviewed, rather than what these witnesses from the military police testified to?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report is based on looking at the regulations, and based on a certain amount of evidence which I gathered from looking at the documents I did look at, from which I drew those conclusions. That is -- that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we discussed yesterday that the significant ones, the key ones are referenced in your report, and the testimonies of those witnesses are not -- I'm just trying to understand that, therefore, you primarily relied on those sources of information, the documents that you had and you referred to, rather than the testimonies of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You referred to your report, the rules of the military police, which is P880, a document that this Chamber is very familiar with. Now, did you know that General Lausic testified that there was dual chain of command contemplated in that article, one going to the military police administration, under Article 8 of the rules, and one going to the commanders of the Military District or the highest HV commander in the area by function under Article 9. Were you aware of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the testimony, but I'm aware of the two rules, the Article 8 and Article 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, based on your review would you agree with General Lausic that there was such a dual chain of command in -- at least in P880 in those regulations, one under Article 8 going to the military police administration, and one under Article 9 going to the HV?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I comment on that, I would just like to see Article 8 and Article 9, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course. I think it is my mistake, I didn't ask for it to be pulled up. I apologise; I thought it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: P880, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I don't want to interrupt. If could I have a page cite where Mate Lausic used the phrase "dual chain of command," I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can look for it at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't think it's -- I think maybe the words -- I think the evidence was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, these words, of course, are not without importance, especially if you ask someone whether he would be right --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I accept that, Your Honour. And for the purpose of my question, it's not -- I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, would you agree that Articles 8 and 9 contemplate two separate chains of commands?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. But one is defined by regular -- one is constrained to regular military tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, no, I accept that. But there are two separate chains; right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two separate linkages. I think we need to be careful before we throw around this word "chain of command" before we quite understand where we are going. It solves the problem. Perhaps I may just put a little background on this from a military perspective. It solves the problem of the alternative chain of command which is clearly shown on that, on the organigram, where the military police are commanded by military police administration which goes into directly the MOD rather than through the Chief of Staff. And this enables, Article 9 enables the coordination and cooperation that General Feldi showed on his -- on his organigram to exist so that military police units engaged in their regular or daily military police tasks could be properly integrated into the operational part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to D267. This is a document you briefly addressed with Mr. Cayley yesterday. You were asked questions about and shown some portion of this document. I want to draw your attention to some others that were not referred to in court. Now, you were shown page 4, paragraph 10. And the transcript reference which I think could be helpful for everyone to pull up is 24175, lines 1 to 4. And, General, you will not have the benefit of that on the screen, so I will read it to you. Mr. Cayley showed you the middle portion of paragraph 10 and said, to refer to the: "I appoint Major Ivan Juric ..." and then skipped straight to the last sentence to elicit your comments and asked you: "The commanders of the 72nd VP battalion and the 73rd VP battalion shall be subordinate to Major Ivan Juric?"

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: An answer to that question, at 24175, 7 to 11, was that Major Juric had been placed in command of those battalions. Now, General, I just wanted to give you an opportunity to look at the paragraph more carefully rather than those -- especially the parts that were skipped because I noticed that Mr. Cayley skipped over the part where it says Mr. Juric was appointed to assist in commanding and organising the activities of the 72nd and 73rd --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry if ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It has just been pointed out that you've just skipped three words, "group of officers." "I appoint Major Juric and a group of officers ..." That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to avoid words like "skipping." Left out is more neutral. Let's try and keep everything neutral, and let's try to be as precise as possible in quoting. Mr. Hedaraly, would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: My question ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: My question, General, is commanding, and assisting in commanding are two different things; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were you aware that General Lausic testified - and I have a transcript reference for my colleagues, it's 15239 - testified that he delegated to Major Juric a portion of his responsibilities under Article 8. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And used the expression as his "ears and eyes on the ground," whereas you used the directed telescope analogy. Now were you also aware that this Chamber has received evidence from a military police member of the 72nd VP Battalion who rejected the proposition that Mr. Juric was the commander of the 72nd Battalion in August 1995 and stated that Mr. Juric was merely a coordinator? Were you aware of that, because I didn't see it in your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who gave that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that's at transcript reference 10348. Now if we now go -- if we're still on D267, I want to show you item 3, which I don't believe you discussed yesterday, which is on the first page. I'm sorry, the second page in the English. And we see here the last portion of item 3, and you can read the whole item, of course. I just want to focus on the last sentence. "Within the daily operational chain of command, commanders of VP battalions" - which would include the 72nd and 73rd - "shall be subordinated to commanders of the HV Military Districts." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And who has written that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is written by Mr. Lausic, I believe. But I will look at the last page. It is by Mr. Lausic. We can go to page 5, last page in English, if you want to look for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I can further tell that you General Lausic testified that for the purpose of this order, operational chain of command referred to the same functions as the regular military tasks according to Article 9 of the rules. That's at 15257.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is what he means by the daily operational chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that D267 also seems to contemplate two separate chains of command? They are subordinated for -- within the daily operational chain of command to the HV and also in part through Mr. Juric for other tasks?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that he is giving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just go back. And I just had the opportunity to look at the premise put out by my learned colleague concerning Mr. Simic said. And in page 31, line 23, Mr. Hedaraly said: "Were you also aware that this Chamber received evidence from a military police member of the 72nd MP Battalion who rejected the proposition that Mr. Juric was the commander of the 72nd Battalion in August of 1995 and stated that Mr. Juric was merely a coordinator? Were you aware of that because I didn't see it in your report?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now are you challenging that that is what Mr. Simic said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Chamber should turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, page 10348 the testimony of Mr. Simic, the question and the answer at line 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. If you would just give me a second to find it. You said 10.000 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 10348. JUDE ORIE: Just one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It starts at page 13, the whole exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10348. I am there. And lines, you said ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: 13 to 23, would be the full ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer, at least, gives some more details and also gives some areas where apparently Mr. Simic is not fully aware of certain aspects of it. And I think it would have been appropriate to summarise it, not just by quoting one or two words but by giving a proper reflection of what the gist of the evidence of Mr. Simic, in this respect, was. Now, very practical question. Mr. Kehoe, do you want to deal with the matter in re-examination, or would you expect Mr. Hedaraly to -- to revisit this issue but now on the basis of a bit more detailed or at least a more nuanced reflection of the testimony of Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't believe that the General has any frame of reference because I'm not sure he actually saw that. So I'm -- I don't know if -- I'll leave it to the Chamber's discretion if that additional information assists the General in any regard. I just am concerned by this summarisation of something that when I go back -- we go back and look at it simply is not present in the record. That's my concern. But as a practical matter, and, again, Mr. President, I leave it to your discretion on how to you address it with General Deverell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just to alleviate any concern that my learned colleague has, I -- I apologise for having summarised perhaps not completely accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to the parties. Of course, the word "commander" and word "coordinator," but there not in general terms, but coordinator of certain operations or actions that Mr. Simic is not aware of or familiar with appear in -- and so some words appear. At the same time, it is not a nuanced summary of what the witness said. I leave it in your hands, Mr. Hedaraly, if you want to revisit the matter; and if not, I take it that Mr. Kehoe would be fully capable of dealing with the matter in re-cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I just add one thing, Mr. President. My concern of course on the fullness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. I give an opportunity to Mr. Hedaraly to re-visit the matter in a more nuanced way. If he doesn't you have an opportunity to do that. We leave it at that for this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Really, the only -- the main point I was trying to make, General, is that you did not consider the evidence of Mr. Simic in reaching your conclusions; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. May I refer back to that -- that order, because I was going to make a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm still going to discuss other portions of it.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you want to make that comment now, or ...

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is it related the last question, or is it a general --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a general comment which perhaps may be helpful at this moment before we go on to other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could just scroll down, or if the page could be scrolled down, please. I'm sorry, scrolled up. There is a part in this where he refers to assisting with command and then several lines later he says the units are subordinated. There is an element in all this, Your Honour, and again this is context, if I may. As a senior officer I would regard that as a very, very badly written order. Because it is ambiguous. What he says there is a nonsense. You cannot assist but be made -- made the commander. He may have been referring to the other people assisting. I can understand why he would want Major Juric to assist, although quite how that is done, I'm not sure. But there is a complete contradiction there. And you see that contradiction then come down and the -- the part I'm looking at now, paragraph 3 of the order, where he uses the phrase, line one, two, three, four, five, six, "within the daily operational chain of command." Now that phrase itself, I believe - and I think people have accepted - actually talks of or refers to Article 9 which is nothing to do with a chain of command. It is to do with the integration of the military police into the operational -- into the operational organisation for regular military tasks. And those are all the standard ones of route marking, route clearing, minor disciplinary -- dealing with minor disciplinary problems and general good order of the force which is laid out in -- in the reference in more -- in one of the other references in more detail. My point is, that actually it's a very ambiguous order. And one needs to be very careful before we draw certain conclusions, conclusions as in, I am certain this is what it meant. That was my point, and I hope, perhaps that might have assisted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly. Have you another four minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I -- I think we can have the break now. I think it's a good time. We will come back to this order after the break anyways. But now is as good a time as another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break, and we will resume at half past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, we were discussing D2670 [sic] order on the screen, and you've provided some commentary regarding how it was ambiguous, in your view, when we left off. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go now to page 4, paragraph 12 under the heading: Commanding and reporting system. And again the last three lines of that section which appear on the following page were shown to you. I don't know if you wish to look at them again now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Why don't we go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: To refresh your memory. Mr. Cayley discussed to comment on the last three lines: "The commanders shall submit their requests." Do you remember that discussion yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to go back to the previous page, please, and look at the first paragraph under that heading at the bottom of the page. "Within the daily operational chain of command commanders of military police battalions" - which includes the 72nd and the 73rd, as well as the companies listed there - "shall be subordinated to the commanders of the HV Military Districts." So that's the second time we see that in this document now. And if we turn over the page. "And they shall report to them in writing and at briefings on a daily basis." Now, you were asked to comment on the last three lines. I wanted to give you a chance to look at more than that portion of this document. Do you agree that this document, however ambiguous it may be, seems to suggest that reports would be sent both to the military police administrations and to the HV commanders?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just scroll up again to the other page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If Mr. Registrar can assist.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says specifically within the daily operational chain of command and we've had that discussion, and I would suggest that means for regular police tasks that those reports and returns go to the -- the military headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And other reports would go to the military police administration, or perhaps the same ones?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or perhaps the same ones. If it wasn't part of a regular military task, then -- if it was something else which was to do with their administration, pay, whatever, conditions of service, then it would go up the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And only -- according to this document, within that chain, right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday you will recall Mr. Cayley also showed you two documents which were not copied to General Cermak. We can look at them again, if you want. I noted that there were also not copied to any HV commanders. I don't know if you remember. If you want to look at them again.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, I'd like to look at them again, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. The first one was D789, which was an order. And if we can go to the last page where the addressees are listed. Can you see here that that order was not copied to any of the HV commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. And then the report was D791. And, similarly, if we go to the bottom of that page, we see that it's delivered to the addressees. And if we go up to the top of the page now, we'll see the addressees being military police, various sections or departments of the military police administration. So this report which was not copied to General Cermak was also not copied to any other HV commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now you cannot exclude for the possibility that this information was also sent to General Cermak, General Gotovina, or another HV officer. In a different communication, for example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you answer the question. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, there's got to be some kind of basis for that question. I mean, it's a -- it's asking the witness to essentially speculate as to whether or not these documents -- when he's actually asked the witness to point out that they're not copied to any HV commanders, and now asking the witness to speculate about whether they could possibly have been sent to these individuals when they're not even on the address list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, if you would ask the witness whether he could exclude for the possibility that this document was sent to me at the time, then I take it that would be difficult for him to exclude a possibility. Therefore, I would agree that we need a kind of a basis which brings the copy to be sent to, for example, General Cermak, as you said, within the ambit of the real world.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was not clear, and I apologise to my learned friends --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was referring to the information contained in that document, rather than the document itself. That it -- could have been sent in another fashion in another report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We discussed various possibilities of reporting earlier, looking at D267.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same would apply as far as the content is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's only -- I mean, I think the point is even stronger, Your Honour, that you're making. I mean, now, we're in the realms of total speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, if there would have been no objection to the question and, of course, there are two possibilities, either that the witness says, I can't exclude that. In that case, the Chamber, of course, would -- we're not a jury. We would understand that not being able to exclude something is if not at zero probative value, perhaps at 0.001. The other possibility is that the witness would have told us something about it, why he would know for sure that it wasn't, or that he would know for sure that it was. And then, of course, we would have listened to what he apparently knows about it. And, therefore, Mr. Hedaraly, the question, whether the witness has any knowledge on whether this document may or the content of the document may have been brought to the attention of the witness would have been a question to be preferred, because it would be perfectly clear from the first answer whether the witness has any knowledge which would assist us or not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yesterday, when commenting on this document, you stated that: "It talks about something they did without informing him." That was based just on the fact that this document was not copied to him; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You don't in fact know whether or not he was informed of the information here --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going back again to the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not the same question. Do you have any knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear. Then there's no need to ask any further questions on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, there is not. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you see any -- any documents from General Gotovina regarding the reporting from the military police; for example, him complaining about not receiving reports on time?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing those documents, but I may have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. On that question, and I don't know if we want to do this in the presence of the witness, because I have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what you are going raise Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I'm raising ago issue concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I take it you have now considered whether or not when you explain do us what you're going to raise whether it could be appropriately done in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, I think, you know, caution being my guide, it may be best to raise my objection at this point regarding that past question by the Prosecutor to the Chamber alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, under those circumstances, I have to ask you, Mr. Deverell, to follow Madam Usher and to leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I'm not going to ask you whether you understand any English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may address the Chamber, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My concern about this question and there are other questions that, likewise, fall into this category, but this seems to be quite salient in page 42, line 18, discussing reporting to the military police and General Gotovina complaining about not receiving reports on time. And the issue of whether or not he saw any reporting in that regard. I would like to know, Mr. President, I submit this is a proper request by the Defence and by the Chamber as to what the good-faith basis is for asking a question like that. Because I would suspect there is no document in possession of the OTP, and I certainly can be educated on that, but we have not seen it. And I submit that the Defence hasn't seen it. So if you're asking a question about reporting from General Gotovina regarding the military police, there has to be some good-faith basis for that question as opposed to just throwing it out and seeing what the answer might be. Now I highlight this question in particular, but there are other questions that fall into that category as well. Is there some aspect of this that is unknown to the Defence, i.e., that there was reporting by the military police to General Gotovina during this period of time? Now, with that query or series of questions in that regard, I turn it over to the Trial Chamber to ask the Prosecution what the good faith basis is for this line of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I am more than happy to acquiesce to Mr. Kehoe's request. My question was regarding any documents indicating the timing of the receipts of the reports. And I was specifically on my mind had -- wasn't going to show it to the witness because he said he had no knowledge, but I was referring to P2194 which, unless I have misread it, is a warning from General Gotovina regarding the timing of the receipt of reports because it may be addressed at the wrong place, and, therefore, there is some delay, with the caveat that have I now summarized it, so perhaps not 100 percent right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me say the following. We hear the testimony of an expert witness who mainly focuses on documentary material and, to some extent, at least who is also aware of some of the testimony this Chamber received. Now, if a witness says something about a document and says, Well, General Gotovina was not informed about it, of course, this is understood by the Chamber as the witness looking at the documents, seeing that the document reveals no information whatsoever that it would have been copied to. That's how -- I don't know how a jury functions. I never was on a jury, so I do not know whether my brain would function in any other way. But that is the context in which this evidence is received. And then if would you say, But you say he was not informed, but do you actually know? Of course, that question makes only sense if there is any reason, first of all, to believe that what the witness said was anything more than what he deduces from the document; and, second, that he would have any knowledge, own observation, et cetera, which would justify to spend time on additional questions to be put to the witness, in order to elicit all the information he may have on the case. That is some general observation. Well, if you ask a witness totally without a foundation whether he has any knowledge, where we would not expect him to have any knowledge, that's a waste of the time, but, at the same time, also not a reason to -- well, to be too much upset about, apart from the waste of time, of course, that's certainly a reason for being upset. But I tried to explain how the Chamber understands and appreciates the evidence in the context of the witness which appears before us. It might have been totally different if it would have been someone who was there at the time, who's commenting on documents but may have some additional knowledge about what happened in reality as well. Here, it has not been established, apart from what the witness told us about his experience in the former Yugoslavia, that he has any specific knowledge going beyond what he saw in the documents and what he has heard and read, in terms of the testimony given by other witnesses. May this be guidance for you, Mr. Hedaraly, to keep focussed on what we could realistically expect from this witness. And for the Defence not -- well, to -- to save then a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
