utterances.text: Thank you for the guidance, Mr. President. I think the Chamber can understand this witness also draws some very broad conclusions sometimes based on documents. So simply asking him he had considered -- had seen any of that evidence. And that was all. I wasn't going to go into any more detail. And he answered that he didn't have knowledge of it, and I was glad to move on, not to waste the Chamber's time. But have I kept that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have done that several times, Were you a wear of this? Were you aware of that? And I didn't hear any objections about that because it enables the Chamber to assess what this expert witness has considered and what he has not considered in writing his report and drawing his conclusions. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, if we are going to go into this exhibit, P2194, it's outside the indictment period. This is 15 November and was not on Prosecutor's witness list either to be used. Exhibit list, excuse me, to be used. But I trust that -- the nodding of my learned friend across the well is that we're not going to go into this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I have understood the Chamber' guidance correctly, I will not be going into that document, nor was I planning to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you have understood it correctly or not, but apparently you are determined not use it, and that's what -- that was the matter to be considered and determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deverell, you earlier said you had nothing to hide. The Chamber has nothing to hide either, but if you want to know what we discussed in your absence, the transcript is available to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- after. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We finished dealing with D267, which were the 2 August order that we saw that you had claimed was ambiguous, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Which now takes us to D47, which is the order from General Lausic, cancelling D267. Were you aware of that -- were you aware that relationship between D47 and D267, because I have not seen it in your report.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me look, and I'll be able to tell you. Yes, I think I am. I think I am. Could you scroll down, please. Yes, I do. The phrase "the degree of combat readiness shall be maintained," I remember, as a specific part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe I was asking whether you remembered -- were you aware of the relationship between this order and D267. I'm asking you this question because I didn't see it in your report.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I am -- I am aware of the relationship. If I'm not, I'm sure you will tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was simply asking you a question about whether you knew or not. You can see that "I hereby order" at the bottom of the page in English and --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- it says to invalidate item 1 of the order, strictly confidential. And the number that you see there is the one for D267.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And other provisions of this document, you will recall, cancel various portions of D267. And if you were not aware of that, well, you are now. And so it took us -- so on 14th of August, this went back to the general situation, having cancelled D267, the general situation under Articles 8 and 9. The last page of this document, paragraph 14, the last sentence: "In daily operational command, subordinate the commanders of the newly established platoons and company of the Knin military police to the most senior HV commander in the zone of responsibility and send the daily report to them." Were you aware, sir, that General Lausic testified that the Knin Company commander would come under the garrison command, as that would be the highest HV command in the area. Were you aware of that testimony by Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that testimony by Mr. Lausic. Is this -- is it for daily tasks?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is for -- right. And did he say under the command, or ... as I haven't seen the -- the document, perhaps before I comment I should be able to see that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just wonder if you were aware of it or not, that there is some -- I don't want to show you a statement of another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, you asked whether the -- Mr. Deverell was aware that General Lausic testified, and then you touched upon the content of his testimony. If you would have asked him, are you aware that he testified on this matter, then we could have left it as it was. But since you now summarise what the testimony was, if you want an answer to that question and the witness already answered it, but then said, Well, I'd like to verify first, in order to be sure that my answer is accurate or not. So there are two options. Either you should say the Chamber should ignore the answer, the question should not have been put by me in this way; or you give an opportunity to Mr. Deverell to look at it, or to summarise it in such a way that Mr. Cayley sits down again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I make some observations and I'll talk in neutral terms, Your Honour, because I think you'll probably know what I'm referring to. But we also know of course the difficulty in Mr. Hedaraly putting that evidence in that manner is the witness was cross-examined. And without going into the details of that cross-examination there was actually specific cross-examination on this particular provision by Mr. Kay. And what I would respectfully submit to the Court is that if the evidence is going to put in this way, and we have been around this buoy before, then the totality of the evidence should be put to the witnesses and not just in isolation. I know you will probably say to me, Well, do that in re-examination, Mr. Kay. But the problem with that is the consequence of simply putting half of the evidence or a quarter of the evidence is that it ends up with me today or tomorrow having to go back to that transcript and having to do an extensive re-examination on the evidence that the witness gave when Mr. Kay cross-examined him. So my submission would be is that either Mr. Hedaraly puts all of the evidence to this witness, or he simply asks, Are you aware of this; no. And then moves on. Because asking this witness to agree with what General Lausic said without actually putting what General Lausic said in its entirety is unfair and it's misleading and I don't really think helps the Court, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I make two observations in this respect. As I said earlier, you can't ask a witness whether he agrees or not with the testimony on the basis of just a very short summary. That -- I do, however, not fully agree with you, Mr. Cayley. I think it's for a cross-examining party can rely on what it considers to be reliable and credible evidence and may choose for that purpose either evidence in cross-examination or evidence given in chief. And, of course, then for the other party, they still to complete that picture, especially if the evidence is contradictory and not knowing whether -- what the evaluation of the Chamber of that evidence will be. Under those circumstances, it's not -- it's not prohibited to put not all of the evidence, of course, in a situation where another interested party can put other parts of that evidence to the witness. At the same time, Mr. Hedaraly, if we do not find ourselves in such a situation; for example, if the witness in cross-examination has not said something different or just clarified, then, of course, it's a waste of time not to put all of it right away to the witness, because otherwise we would not -- we would not receive the evidence, which assists us best in making the determinations we will finally have to make. So the situation -- I do not fully agree with you in every respect, Mr. Cayley, but I would say 70 per cent of it is good enough for Mr. Hedaraly to carefully think it over, if he does not put all of the evidence in relation to a certain matter to the witness; but he is not under all circumstances obliged to put it all to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Perhaps I can simplify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, were you aware of General Lausic's testimony regarding the relationship between the Knin Military Police Company and the Knin garrison command?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sorry, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, may I take it from this way in which you followed up the objections and the observations by the Chamber, that you would invite the Chamber to ignore the earlier "yes" by -- as an answer, and I will be very specific there --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I took the first option proposed to me by the Chamber earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the Chamber will not consider the evidence by this witness where he agreed with your -- and let me -- if you could assist me in finding the right page and number so that we are ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's actually 49:4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I noticed earlier that there is an slight discrepancy between the line numbering in some of the systems. Yes, the -- everything else asked from this witness and the further inquiries he made into what the content of the testimony is, the Chamber will ignore that, and the Chamber will pay attention only to the fact that this witness was not aware of the testimony of General Lausic, regarding the relationship between the Knin Military Police Company and the Knin garrison commands, where he said that he was not aware of it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, you were also asked yesterday a question by Mr. Kehoe at transcript 24193 where he suggested to that you General Lausic took a significant step in ensuring his personal control and that of the military police over controlling military police criminal investigations by requiring reporting to Major Juric. Do you remember that question by Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that Mr. Simic, who was a crime investigation police officer, testified that he did not report to Major Juric, that he came under the command of the HV and that crime investigation were part of his daily activity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like a transcript reference, page, line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would also like an opportunity to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: P967, paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly. Well, it -- under normal circumstances, I would -- I would take the view that every party is expected to summarise any piece of evidence he wants to put to the witness in a most accurate way, and that unless there's any reason to believe that there might be mistakes there. However, in view of the experience of today on several matters, I think the best way to proceed is, first, to ask the witness whether he is aware of evidence without yet summarizing it, just touch upon what it is about, rather than what it is, and then immediately give the source to the -- to the Defence so that they can immediately check whether any summary they could expect if the witness answered that question by yes is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I just can interject. At this point what the Prosecutor alluded to in the -- with regard to that testimony is not in evidence, and I direct the Chamber to -- and what I'm say something is he just referred to paragraph 16 and P967. I address the Chamber to the proofing note for the witness at P968, line -- paragraph 4, where he notes in paragraph 16: "It is stated that the commanders of the units in the field reported to the Military District command about the committed crimes. I cannot confirm that claim because I have no knowledge about it." So, what he put was -- in paragraph 16 of P967 when he was called by the Prosecutor, the witness backed off of it in P968, paragraph 4 of the supplemental witness statement, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any -- it's still for the Chamber to decide. It is not automatically that everything a witness stays later makes the earlier statement in every respect and under all circumstances not to be used. It will depend on many circumstances, although we would, as a starting point, accept if a witness -- if a witness corrects his statement. We'll look at all kind of circumstances, such as under what circumstances the statement was taken, under what circumstances the -- the supplementary statement is, or the corrections are made. At the same time, as I said before, it may -- in most of the cases be a waste of time just to put half of the testimony of a witness to a new witness. But again, the first question I would have asked of this witness is whether he is aware of the testimony by Mr. Simic on a certain matter. Because if the answer is no, then we can just avoid all these kind of discussions which lead us to nowhere. So, could you please rephrase your question, just asking this witness, without summarizing the content, but just referring to the subject matter of the testimony, whether he has seen it and whether he has considered it when drafting his report and forming his opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one comment on that regard. The statement that counsel read in paragraph 16 of 967 is not in evidence. It hasn't been 92 ter'd because -- pardon me using Rule 92 ter in the verb. But has not been admitted in evidence pursuant to 92 ter because that portion of the statement he did not acknowledge that he would say this or attest to were he asked those same questions in court. Accordingly, that portion of paragraph 16 alluded to by Mr. Hedaraly is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have to consider whether it is or it is not -- what I see in this document, some portions were specifically taken out. For example, paragraph 17 is not in evidence. It has been blackened out. And therefore before ever -- but, again, that, we're not discussing at this moment exactly. I invited Mr. Hedaraly to rephrase his question in such a way that if there is no need to have all this trouble to avoid it. Mr. Hedaraly, could you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kehoe, in addition, you will understand that not on my mind I remember every single detail of what the attestation was about, not being prepared on these kind of details in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I appreciate that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, were you aware of Mr. Simic's testimony with regard to the reporting of crimes -- of crime investigations to Major Juric or not?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you're invited to, if we are in a similar situation, put the first question, as I already asked you before. I think my last observation was if you would please introduce the matter in the way in which you did it now, not in the way you did it earlier, because that really could, I'm not saying will, but could save quite a bit of time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to turn briefly to -- in your report when you discuss the crimes that took place in Sector South and the fact that General Cermak would have undoubtedly been aware of their occurrence and that there were times when there were discrepancy between what the internationals reported and the official version of the Croatian government and that in those cases he was not trying to mislead the internationals but he was simply accepting the version that was given to him. And you gave the example of Grubori, for example. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the portion of the interview General Cermak gave to the Office of the Prosecutor regarding an argument that he may have had with General Tolj regarding those crimes?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see it before I say that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. It's at P2525, and it's page 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you also give me the page reference in the report where the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's towards the end. I think it's page 55 -- there's a -- that discussion is at several places. Page 55 is one example. And just for the full context, if we can go to the page before, just so that we can see the full answer and the question. Go to bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You said line 31, there is a question: "Who else were you not popular with in the military? You mention Mr. Susak. Who else?" If we can go to the next page, it starts at page -- at line 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't mean to interrupt counsel, but my client needs to be able to read -- or the accused need to be able to read these things that are being read into the record, if he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The problem that I alluded yesterday, and I checked overnight, is for some reason there is no full B/C/S translation. There is a mixed B/C/S-English, and we're trying to resolve that. And I do apologise to those following in B/C/S. I tried to have the video-clip so that they could listen to the original, but there is some technical issues, I was told, and it is not synced properly. So I didn't want to use it, but the witness asked to look at it, so I really apologise for that. I will read it slowly so that everyone can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm guided by Your Honours decision in this. I'm not quite sure how which should proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers it very unfortunate that we do not -- cannot give, at this moment, direct access to the accused but fully accepts that if this is verified or, if on the basis of further discussions with your client, that you would like to revisit the matter or that you would claim that Mr. Hedaraly has not appropriately put to the witness what was in evidence, that you have a full opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I certainly don't want to interrupt, but so the Chamber understands, we engage with the clients as all Defence counsel do, and it is simply a matter when something comes up often times they want to give us a note or say something about a particular comment to put it in context. And it's in that in vein and not to interrupt counsel's line of inquiry that I'm raising this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and even if during this hearing you would like to further discuss or need a break for that purpose, it will be given to you, because everything that is available to us to -- to counterbalance this unfortunate situation will be -- will be given to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me read from the document for the record and for the translation. "I also had a telephone duel with General Tolj. General Tolj was in charge of political work and the media as well, and he was also the spokesperson of the Ministry of Defence during Storm. Oftentimes in the media in Slobodna Dalmatia and other papers, I criticised the situation. I said that things are happening and it's actually a shame, that some things for Croatia and for the Croatian state. In Slobodna Dalmatia I said that some members of the Croatian military are to blame for what happened and that some of the blame must be put on the military commanders because they have to check the military on the ground and that not everything can be done that people were doing. "And two days later there was an article in the newspaper where General Tolj was quoted saying that on the ground the Croatian military isn't doing anything, that these were some civilians who were dressed in military uniforms, looting and burning. And there was a huge article, my article was tiny, his was a huge article, and it said, The crimes in this area are not being committed by the Croatian military according to reports by the military police but that this was being carried out by civilians who were dressed up, which was not true. And I called him on the telephone. I told him, saying, You're sitting there in Zagreb, you don't even know what the situation on the ground is. And the truth is what I'm telling you, I'm telling you now. Such articles don't really help anybody, they're just negative because hiding and lying won't help anybody. And I said some nasty things to him, that ... he said, Well, don't be upset with me, you know that ... there are people higher up. So, then he sent me basically ... and that was the last I heard from him." Had you seen that exchange before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that piece. I have seen several bits of the transcript of General Cermak being interviewed. But I don't recall that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can I ask you how did you select which portions of the transcripts to read? Because I know they're voluminous --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just -- I mean, I selected because I was looking through, and I was looking for things which interested me. Clearly, I didn't see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you were flipping through the transcripts just generally looking for information?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for particular words, particular things which were of interest. I mean, that's the way I doing my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I can just tell you that you the date of the newspaper article that is referenced is 7 September. The article is in evidence as D59. And I don't know if have you seen the article itself or not.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen several articles, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't -- I mean, for the purposes of my question -- if you need to refer back to it, let me know.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm happy to focus on this particular piece of paper at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So on that occasion, and I appreciate that's in September, around -- a few days after the 7th, General Cermak is arguing with General Tolj regarding who's committing the crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So if, after this conversation, General Cermak told internationals that crimes were committed by non-soldiers or civilians dressed in military uniforms, would that change your conclusion regarding the fact that he was simply accepting a version without knowing really what was happening?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think this -- I don't think this tells you that he knew what was happening. I think this -- this has a very interesting -- you could -- you could look at many countries to find that this sort of conversation was going on and the times of great national crisis and stress of people between those who sit in the headquarters and those who are on the grounds. And -- and you may have noticed -- well, you were reading that I was smiling while I was reading this because I think, you know, being a soldier we have all experienced this. It -- it highlights the -- the problem that I alluded earlier. And I would just like that make this comment to add context to it. The problems of having a person who de facto becomes a spokesman and somebody who has command responsibility. I don't think it, to me, changes the issue that Cermak, who consistently is being given general information about crimes by Brigadier General Forand, and you will remember that he asks for evidence, and we may be discussing that at some stage in the future, where General Cermak asks the letter where he talks about insinuations. And General Forand and I make a comment in my report that I was surprised that the United Nations or UNCRO, that their staff work was, I would say, not particularly high standard at the time because they had not provided General Cermak with specific evidence beforehand. And that he was dealing in generalities. It doesn't change my view that at Grubori he chose to give the version which was that which he felt was the true one. And because he a television camera there, I guess he wanted to make the best of what he felt was actually, at the time, a success. The capture, killing of some renegade Chetniks. Now, the truth of the issue is another matter. And we may discuss that later. But what I'm trying to say is that this, to me, doesn't change -- the fact that he has had this row on 7th of September doesn't actually mean that what he says afterwards is being influenced by General Tolj. It might do. It would be a reasonable assumption. But I -- I guess that there will be another, an alternative view which I might take that he continues to act as the spokesman and he continues to give a view of incidents which reflect his country's view in the absence of specific information which subsequently he gets, as I recall, from United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just to go back on your answer because it was quite lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you talked about this common occurrence between someone on the field and someone in an office in Zagreb, General Cermak would be the one who would have the better information than General Tolj since he was in Knin and General Tolj was in Zagreb. Is that a reasonable interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not actually a reasonable interpretation, and this is the paradox. Because sometimes the person who is sitting at the heart of the communication system will have better information than somebody who has got a relatively narrow view of what he sees in -- in -- within his precise area. So one must be careful before we make that -- that distinction as a matter of course. In my -- in my personal experience, normally the person on the ground understands what's happened on ground more clearly but may not be able to put the -- may not be able to put it into its context in a way that somebody further back with more information can. But we're in very difficult areas here, and it depends on personalities and your command and control system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me talk briefly about a few topics, and I will address them fairly rapidly and none of those are issues that we necessarily deal -- have to deal with in some detail. Perhaps we may decide to, but at this moment -- And the first one is in your report, at page 15, when you are discussing the structure of garrisons generally and what they usually are limited to. One of the examples that you give at line 9 is that they would be responsible for traffic control. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, would check-points fall under traffic control?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could do. Although, I'm sorry, just can I clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- the exact phrase is within line 9: "Within their garrison such as regulations for the use of facilities." Regulations, therefore, for traffic control for speed limits. So it is more about -- that line is more about -- the regulations is more about having a 30 mile an hour -- or 30 kilometre an hour speed limit, and where it might be than the physical placing of check-points, their regularity, when they are to be, what they are to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But check-point would regulate traffic as well.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the check-point might be the means of regulating traffic. What I refer to here is the instructions, the regulations that that check-point would be monitoring or imposing. So one is -- one is, as it were, procedure, that the -- the production of a procedure; and the other is the imposition of that procedure, the ensuring that that procedure is followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And at page 43 of your report, you talk generally about freedom of movement. And you then cite a few documents, suggesting that General Cermak's granting freedom of movement was unclear. You refer to one early example from 8/9 August and the one from 7 October as well. Those are the two examples that you use in your report.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, this Chamber has also received evidence and reports of internationals which showed that, upon either a phone call to General Cermak or sometimes even a threat of a phone call to General Cermak, they were allowed to go through a check-point when they were initially stopped. Did you review that evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have some kind of citation for this. Can you ground that in an exhibit or a transcript or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'll give a few examples from the ECMM reports P511, P818, P1294 and the testimony is generally of, for example, Eric Hendriks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you see any such documentation, General, and if you did, can you tell us why you didn't reference it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I did. I know that freedom of movement increasingly became a reality. But to go to my words, if I may, line 12. "His name and authority did not always carry much weight." Now, implicit in "did not always," I meant to show that sometimes it did. What I was demonstrating there was that his authority, much as it might have been, did not spread particularly far. There was still evidence that people didn't know who General Cermak was, or would not accede to a pass or the use of his name. At all stages in this particular part, I'm talking about a situation which was very unclear, and I'm trying to identify that the -- that the simple -- the simple assessment that General Cermak had authority because he wrote the order, that even if some people obeyed that order, it did not go very far. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deverell, would you mind if I took you back to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you had considered evidence to the effect that, when initially stopped at check-point, whether a phone call or the suggestion that a phone call could be made changed the attitude of the person who stopped and a phone call to General Cermak? Did you -- are you aware of, and did you consider it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me, Your Honour. I am aware of it because it rings a bell. I was not specific -- I can't specifically quote an example. And I -- I chose not to produce a footnote, an example of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was part of what you said when I said mainly, that sometimes it did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just raise one issue. And this has happened several times. I mean, we ask for a frame of reference for a particular line of questioning, and our procedure has been throughout this trial to disclose the exhibits that were going to be used in cross-examination. And P511, P518, P1294 that just were cited in response to the question raised by Mr. Cayley have not been disclosed as documents that are going to be used by the Prosecution. Now, again, maybe I should have raised this when this began, but this is not the first time this has transpired. If we are going properly prepare --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... to start with. The factual information Mr. Kehoe is providing is correct, Mr. Hedaraly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was not planning to use them, Mr. President. Until I was asked to provide a reference, I did not show them to the witness. I simply asked if he was aware of general information with respect to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time you are referring to very specific events, and you are asking about the evidence which shows. And therefore under those circumstances even if you would not intend to use that, the statements or the specific evidence, of course, the first thing you could expect is that the Defence would say, Where do we find that? So, therefore, perhaps you would discuss further, perhaps among the parties, how to deal with these matters. Because I notice that there is a - and I'm looking in both directions - that the flow of evidence is more interrupted than not interrupted, and we should try to find ways to avoid this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You discussed yesterday the order for active defence which was D281, you will recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I have the page reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was in court yesterday you discussed --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think you referred to it in your report as well, but --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- I'm focussing on yesterday. And you were shown the organisational chart on the last page, you will recall?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that organisational chart did not include the Knin garrison, as the Knin garrison command is not an operational entity; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my judgement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you also discussed yesterday, I think Mr. Cayley showed you two elements in that report about the 4th and the 7th Guards Brigades, to be resting in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I've also noticed that we don't see on this organisational chart the 4th and the 7th Guards Brigade. Do you have any knowledge as to why they are not included?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is because, of course, they were not part. They were in reserve, not part of the -- that part of the operation. I mean, that is a judgement I make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you've -- you also noted that this particular order was not copied to the Knin garrison.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And that that surprised you as well.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't surprise me. It -- necessarily that it merely identified -- and I was using this as -- as another part of the proof that Knin garrison was not part of the operational element of Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we look at P1219. And we see there at the second paragraph of a report from General Cermak to the Main Staff: "The Split Military District and the Knin garrison command are in constant coordination." Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What -- what would it mean to be in constant coordination?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would expect to find reports and returns or discussions. Of course, there may have been discussions on the telephone which are not recorded here. There would have been some sign that that coordination was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, this was a report that was in response to the order that we saw yesterday, the last document that was shown to you by Mr. Kuzmanovic. I don't know if you remember it. If you want me to pull it up for you so that ...

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think can I remember it. If I need to pull it up, if I may, I will ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That was an order to the -- remember that the one of mistranslations of Knin garrison, rather than Knin Military District?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That may jog your memory. And that was an order requesting information from all Military Districts and the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this is the response to that -- to that order. And it says -- I read the first sentence already about the constant coordination. And then it continues: "The intelligence assessment regarding this order was made by" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: "... by the chief of the intelligence Department of The Split Military District Command. If we were do submit the same, I would consider it a repetition of work." Now, in your report, at page 30, you said: "More likely, he" -- being General Cermak, "did not have the physical means to do it." Can you tell us what's the basis for that statement that more likely he did not have the physical means, rather than what we see on paper which is that they were in constant coordination and, therefore, it was unnecessary?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I said that he didn't have the physical means to do it was, Your Honour, quite simply, that it enabled me to identify a time or an example when the lack of numbers in his headquarters and the lack of skill sets -- I'm sorry it's a jargon word. The lack of relevant skills would have prevented him from, in my judgement, producing what the chief of the Main Staff wanted. That was -- that was a point that I was trying to draw out. I believe, and I think I -- I said in my report that, of course, there are two interesting aspects here. One is that I'm not entirely certain what the Chief of the Main Staff was doing writing to a subordinate headquarters, where he should have been actually writing to General Gotovina, and it was for General Gotovina to task General Cermak to conduct that particular piece of work. And I -- I suggest that there is some human element in here, and it is General Cermak trying to find a reason why he should not do that work because he was not inclined to do it because he was to busy doing other things. And as we here from the commander Sector South in several of his reports or at least one of his reports, you know, General Cermak is a very busy man. So that -- that would be my -- my view of that slightly looking under the surface of it. I tried to -- to get some reasonable deductions from that -- from that particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: General, thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. We were scheduled to have the break at 3.00. I wonder whether we should take the break first. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment to consult with Mr. Kay, Your Honour, if we take the break now. I would like ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have a break, and we will resume at quarter past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have any further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a few, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I would just like to clarify a few issues that came up during the cross-examination by Mr. Hedaraly. And I would first like to go back to address the active defence order D281.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could put that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I could turn to paragraphs 5.4 and 5.5. Again, that's the active defence order of 9 August 1995. That's page 6 in the B/C/S, I am told. If could you help -- thank you. Okay. Now, General, when we were discussing these two units, and you were asked about the non-presence of these brigades on the organigram. You noted on page 68, line 12: "I believe this is because, of course, they were not part. They were in reserve not part of that operation. This is a judgement I can make." Now, if wee look at 5.4, 5.4 notes that: "Only a -- if we say -- HV 4 Guards Brigade shall be withdrawn from the front line in order to take a break to be replenished and to get ready for further combat activities." Now, in your experience, General, that's R and R, rest and relaxation for the troops; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could be considered to be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the Split Military District commander shall have in reserve one HV 4 Guards Brigade Infantry Battalion. And that's the battalion that was in the Knin barracks. So with regard to the 4th Guards Brigade, we have one battalion that's in reserve, and the rest of the battalion is on rest and relaxation. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether can you call it rest and relaxation, a break and to be replenished, technically. I mean, I don't know what they would have been doing. But I guess that they would have been relaxing by default almost because they were not fully employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were -- were you aware that the 4th Guards Brigade was out of the Split area?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I -- I know -- I know that one was, as it were, organic to Split Military District and one was not. I couldn't remember off the top of my head which one was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's turn our attention to 5.5 which is the comment on the 7th Guards Brigade. And it notes: "HV 7 Guards Brigade shall be withdrawn from the front line in order to rest and replenish and again to get ready for further combat actions -- activities. Split Military District commanders shall have in reserve one HV 4 Guards Brigade company." And I think that should read, if I'm not mistaken --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should read 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the original it is the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think in the original we can agree it says the 7th. If we look at 5.5. I don't speak Croatian but the Arabic numerals are the same, 7 and 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems fair to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In any event, General, again, we have a company of the 7th Guards Brigade -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am also told by Mr. Misetic that this should be a battalion and should not read company, as we see in the document. And we will have that changed and share with our colleagues across the well and upload it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In any event, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think under those circumstances, if there are already two mistakes in one paragraph, that the whole of the translation should be revised, and since it appears as an unrevised translation, proper attention should be paid to it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. In any event, General, we yet another element the 7th Guards Brigade, a portion of them is in reserve and the rest are on rest and relaxation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And by the way, General, that's something you would expect after combat activities, to send your troops out for rest and relaxation away from the area to get them ready for further combat activities. Is it not?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if can I address -- again, I'm going to be jumping around to some issues here. And I would like to go back and talk a little bit about the request by General Cermak of D304, if we can go back and put that on the screen. As we see, this is the 12th of August. It is sent to the Military District Command, and as the president pointed rightly to the attention of the Chief of Staff. And as we turn to page 2 of the English, staying on the B/C/S, we note that it's termed "we request your assistance." And you noted as we turn to the order, the implementation order of D305.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to D305.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is, as you testified, was the order that came out of the Split Military District, and if we turn to page 2 of the English if we can go up a bit. It's handwritten and it's signed for General Gotovina. Now, in explaining this sequence, General, you noted - and this is on page 10 of today's transcript, line 25, going on to page 11: "Did he not ask actually General Gotovina" -- and I think you were meaning to say, He did not ask General Gotovina to write the order for him. "He was not in a position to dictate what -- what General Gotovina gave. He requested, first of all, for manpower. It was a request." Now, you say he made a request because he was not in a position to dictate to General Gotovina under those circumstances what he should do. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention to D818. And this is a document signed by General Gotovina on the 13th of September, 1995, to General Cermak, subject: Request. And if I may read this just briefly, General, and I ask for your assistance in just listening to what I'm going to articulate because I believe that the translation is not completely accurate as well. And we went through the discussion on this document and discussed the correct translation at page 13502, line 16 to 25, to 13503, line 6. And it notes in the way that I understand that it reads in Croatian and the way it was put on the record that I just previously discussed on this request, it says: "General, sir, in the future, please" -- so this is: "General, sir, in the future, please do not issue any authorisation for the movement of members of international military and political organisations and humanitarian organisations like the EC, UNMO, and others, in the direction of Srb-Una railway station and the Bosanski Grahovo-Glamoc- Kupres area, since these areas remain war zones until further notice." Now, in this particular situation as the other was a request by General Cermak to General Gotovina, this is a request by General Gotovina to General Cermak. And it's not an order because under these circumstances with this remit with internationals, General Gotovina was not in a position to dictate to General Cermak what to with the internationals. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Kehoe, we have a difference here between reality and theory. I would say that there was nothing, and I think we've had this conversation before, there was nothing in -- there was nothing that was written down, which changed the subordination of garrison headquarters to a Military District. I think what we have here, however, is mere courtesy. There are two senior Generals. Funny enough the -- the Croatian sort of guidance on -- on human relationships makes a great point of being well-mannered and what I see here, of course, is not an order given. It is request, and it is partly because he wishes General Gotovina -- I'm sorry, he wishes General Cermak to conform and partly because he wishes to give General Cermak the respect that an officer of the same rank deserves. It does actually highlight the difficulty of having an officer of the same rank in a subordinative role. So I think you can draw two conclusions from here. One is that, to my mind, it didn't necessarily change the theoretical subordination, but it actually demonstrates that there was a different relationship between the two of them. A relationship of equal rank which both General Gotovina and General Cermak had to manage. And there is a human dynamic here, which I believe, again, if had I been able to give any context during my replies during the past couple of days, I hope I have been able to, and there is that context here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you have, General, and we're very grateful for that. But the reality, as we look through this, is that they were treating each other as colleagues, not as commander/subordinate relationship. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think de facto, that is it correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might just have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could just show you one last document on this issue of dealing with each other as colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn to D1006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] This document, General, I'm not certain if you have seen this. But it notes that there's going to be an inspection of the Main Staff, and it's going to inspect, if we can look at the -- all ZP units which would be part of the Split Military District which, of course, would theoretically include the Knin garrison. If we could turn next page. And if we look at the addressees on this, it has the entities, including - if we look at the bottom portion of the addressee - the other garrisons that we have in there. But the Knin garrison is missing from that. Could you give us your expert analysis as to why under these circumstances that we would have a separate -- or if there is no inspection of the Knin garrison, or is it something like, again, as colleagues, General Gotovina will take care of these particular garrisons, and his colleague General Cermak would take care of the Knin garrison?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I scroll up a bit. Because if I have seen this, I can't remember the detail. It rings a bell somewhere. But I'm afraid -- I would just like to see the detail, what they are inspecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could go back to page 1. I believe they are expecting [sic] quite a few things.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I can't give a definitive answer, quite clearly. I could only offer one possible reason. I mean, there are several reasons. It may have been missed off, a simple error like that, of course, although I doubt it. It may be, of course, when you go back and look at General Cermak's resources he had in his garrison and the numbers of people and the responsibilities of that garrison, that there was no -- there was nothing inspect. That is -- that is a deduction which could be drawn from there, but I -- I would admit that I'm -- I'm looking at that and making some assumptions. It talks about the compatibility of ZP command and units for command and control. I'm sorry, he didn't have the command and control function. It talks about performance of task in defence of the state border and in control of territory. Now, I know the other garrisons will -- had the same -- the same constraints put upon them in terms of their capacity to be responsible for operations and the rest of it. Whether the garrisons had other resources like a logistics depot of some sort which had to be inspected because of refurbishment equipment, I have no idea. That is the only logical reason I can deduce from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And given the fact that we're in the area of what could be, it could also be that General Gotovina is taking care of those garrisons that has directly got his finger on while allowing his colleague, General Cermak to deal with his particular garrison.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put that impression. You could take that impression away. I mean, I would only answer that a inspection is a relatively neutral thing. It's for the assistance of the Main Staff to identify where there are problems, and I would have been surprised that the Main Staff were -- were happy to have General Cermak dealt with separately. So I think it's -- it's difficult to draw a concrete -- concrete conclusions from this. It may be as you say. It may be something slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if -- if in fact the garrison was a de facto subordination, not a de jure, a de facto subordination. If the Knin garrison was de facto subordinated to General Gotovina, it should have been part of this order.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean de jure?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, if it had been de facto in reality, because we have been talking about the different jobs that General Cermak had done which is not part of the pure garrison rules that you discussed during your remit. But if in fact he had been a de facto garrison under General Gotovina, it should have been part of this orders?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may be misunderstanding exactly how you expressing that question. Could I answer the question I think have you asked me, and then can you come back and tell me whether I have answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is that -- that Knin garrison was de jure subordinated to Split Military District, because that's what the regulations said, and I saw nothing which formally changed that. I believe their that de facto relationship was as two equals of -- two people of equal rank, and that indeed put an atmosphere into that relationship. And indeed as I have said, had I been General Gotovina, I would have been very happy that General Cermak was dealing with some of the problems that we've spent -- we've spent time discussing. I don't believe that the de jure subordination would have enabled the Main Staff -- I'm sorry, I have to go back on that. I'm confusing myself now. What we see here, had there been -- assuming there was de jure subordination, which is my assumption because I have seen nothing to change it, I would wonder why there -- that Knin garrison was not involved in it. I can only come to the conclusion that either there was error in the drafting of the order, which may have been true, or there was some other reason which may have been that actually the Main Staff and General Gotovina knew that there was nothing worthwhile inspecting there, and it would have been a waste of effort. Have I answered the question you asked me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My follow-up question was, or there was a -- another order going down the Knin garrison where an inspection was done parallel to these other garrisons?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that is it an another alternative. And if it -- it was, I'm not aware of it. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. Let us shift gears if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, is there any basis for that? You earlier were rather critical about Mr. Hedaraly to speculate that things might have taken another course without any -- without any basis for that. Is there any reason that there would be an inspection or another order? Or was it just you never know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, I think it is in the spirit of completeness, in the idea that when a military headquarters says that we are going to inspect all units of a command, that would include all units of the command. Now, it could that be this was left out. It could be that because of the unique relationship there was a separate inspection. It could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I cut this short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no specific reason, and we heard from the witness that may be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- my follow up to that, Mr. President, and my good-faith basis is, of course, and it's a question that -- that General Deverell raised on 1219 concerning the inspection of units in the area pursuant to the 21 August 1995 order of the Main Staff, one was sent to the Split Military District and one was sent to the Knin garrison. Now I appreciate the question raised by General Deverell on that score, but it does indicate that there seems to be -- and that's at P1219, for the record. And that does seem to be on the Main Staff level, dealing with these two entities separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I may, General, I would like to go back to the military police, if we can. Again, I apologise for jumping around here, but I will try to get through this as quickly as possible. You were shown D267 by Mr. Cayley and by Mr. Hedaraly. And you noted some confusion in the language concerning the remit and the authority of Major Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could just bring that up very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is -- we can just stay on the front page because I know, general, you know the contents of this document with which you expressed some questions. But this is dated the 2nd of August of 1995 from General Lausic. And I'd like to show you another order that was signed by General Lausic of the same day, D268, which this order, General, addresses Major Juric's taskings directly, unlike the prior order, 267, where we have any number of individuals that are being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we could bring D268 on the screen. If we could just scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as you can see, General, this is an order that is signed on the same day as the prior order with which you had some questions. And the subject is the order of the chief of the Split Military District -- excuse me, of the Main Staff of the military police, and it notes: "Pursuant to an assessed and demonstrated need, with a view to efficient and effective implementation of military police and other ... military police units' zones of responsibility and an effective system of commands, supervision, and provision of professional assistance to the armed forces military police units, I hereby issue the following order ..." And he notes that a group is being named included Major Juric. And I'm interested in the tasks that Major Juric is given by his commander, Major-General Lausic. And if we could go to the -- you see at the bottom, it says Major Ivan Juric's task.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next page. In the first paragraph: "In the command system he is superior to the commanders of the 72nd Military Police Battalion and the 73rd Military Police Battalion with regard to the 73rd Military Police Battalion extending assistance to the 72nd Military Battalion of the Military Police." So he is superior to the commanders there; correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next: "He is responsible for the implementation of all military police tasks in the 72nd Military Police Battalion zone of responsibility." Next paragraph he goes into some coordination that he is responsible for with the MUP and others. I'm interested in the one right after that, that is he authorised to undertake all measures to ensure efficient and effective implementation of military police tasks and the 72nd Military Police Battalion and north OS zones of responsibility. Now, General, based on these two orders together, to the accident that there is any question about who is in charge after your reading of D267, it is clear, is it not, based on the direct taskings given to Major Juric that we just read, that he is the man in charge that Lausic is sending down there on the 2nd of August to be his telescope or his man on the ground, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And he, based on your further dealings or further review of the documents, it is he who is reporting back on a daily basis to Lausic telling him what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the question of command and control about who has command and control of the military police, I would like to show you a series of documents that spread over approximately, oh, I'm going to say several months, if we can, because we are going back until even to the January of 1996. The first is D292. This is a report by General Lausic of the 15th of August, 1995, to General Cervenko, subject: Report of the engagement of the military police units in Operation Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3 in the English, and I will check to see what page it is in the B/C/S. It is page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, General, I am interested in the paragraph right above the bold 2 that reads: The system of preparation. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The system of preparation, planning, control and command at the level of the Split -- excuse me, at the level of the military police administration and the daily operational ordered issued by the commander of the HV Military District and the Main Staff made it possible for the military police to perform all its tasks and for the military police to be engaged in the offensive operations." The initial line, General, says the control and command was at the level of the military police administration. That is the 15th. Let me move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sorry, the rest of that sentence. And the daily operational --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I read that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can just repeat it -- [Overlapping speakers] ... Counsel only mentioned the first -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, it is only Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I've had a rough day, judge. It's tough in the back row.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would rather in the spotlight, Mr. Kehoe. I understand that. Could you please read that paragraph which is on your screen in its entirety so that both gentlemen are happy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to D -- excuse me, D567. Again, this is another report, General, by Major-General Lausic of the 16th of September, 1995, analysing the use of the military police during Operation Storm. And if I can turn to page 2 in the English. And it's also page 2 in the B/C/S. If we can go to the bottom of that page beginning: "The combination."

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I will read it in toto: "A combination of the preparations planning, leading, and commanding of the military police administration and the daily operational commanding by the commanders of the HV Military Districts and the HV Main Staff made it possible to carry out all of the tasks within the competence of the military police and use of the military police units in assault operations." One last example on this score, and that is D978. General, I am not sure if you reviewed this document yet, but this is a report on the work of the military police administration for 1995. Looking back, obviously it is issued in January 1996 under the command of Major-General Lausic, looking back at the activities in 1995. And I would like to turn our attention to page 3. If I can, we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go another page up, please. And if we could go to -- keep going, please. The pagination is a bit off. Just keep going to -- page up, please. It would be the second -- it would be the third English translation page. Two more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I may assist, there are two translations linked. I believe Mr. Kehoe wants the second translation link, page 3 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the page I want that's on the English screen. Thank you very much, counsel. And that's page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, this again reiterates in the bold right above 1.1.4, in the bold, again: "The control and command system at the level of the military police administration and daily operation [sic] command at the level of the commanders ..." And we read through that. Now, General, this is a constant theme by General Lausic, is it not, from the very outset of the documents you reviewed until this in January of 1996, that he, as the commanding officer of the military police, retained command and control over the military police throughout all this. Is it not?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a constant theme, yes. I -- you may be about to direct my attention at the words "daily operational commands."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we move into the area of daily operational commands which you noted for us are activities that are in support of the operation on the ground. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So distinguish those two, what is General Lausic remaining in command and control over?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lausic remains in command and control of the military police under Article -- I think I'm right in quoting under Article 8, the military police administration exercises command and control. This reflects Article 9, if I remember correctly, and I'm sure somebody will tell me if I have got there wrong, which is then supported by the detail of the tasks of the military police, which tasks 3 and onwards, I deduced were the regular tasks. And those are things like minor discipline, the keeping of good order, things like traffic control, all those relatively minor issues which are so important and an operational force is dependant upon. That I believe is what we are looking at in terms of daily operational command, daily operations command. To me - and this may be the answer to your question or not - to me, that emboldened paragraph, when put against Articles 8 and 9, fits. I think it is consistent. It may be that you would agree with me, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I do, General.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, what we have here, General - if we can just synopsise this Article 8 and Article 9 as you just explained - is -- what we have is a vertical subordination between the military police administration down to the ground, and a horizontal coordination between the military police and the, in this case, the Split Military District. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the subordination remains with the vertical line going up to the military police administration, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so. I mean, Article 8 says just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deverell, I may have a few questions, only a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your attention was drawn to P71, the Split Military District diary, General Gotovina says, and I'm now reading the transcript, "that the military police is to take security control, war booty, and take photographs, and make video recordings at the end of the operation. People will be called before military disciplinary courts." Are you aware of any such photographs and video recordings being produced?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I am addressing the parties. Are any of the parties aware of the existence of any photographs or videos produced as a result of what we find in P71?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about, I would say, the advantages, or you testified about the advantages of an independent military police investigating regime. And let me read what you said. You said: "I mean, it's quite simply, really. It's important to have your criminal investigation capability independent of the chain of command, because it might, at some stage, be investigating the chain of command. The chain of command might have, might feel, that they do not want a proper investigation conducted, and therefore, there is a great advantage in having those two separated." And I think this was raised in the context of Mate Lausic taking very significant steps to ensure that the military police and he personally stayed in control of those investigations. Now, you have pointed out the advantage. Have you considered the disadvantage in terms of losing an instrument to fulfil a duty to investigate, if you have reasons to believe that crimes are committed or are about to be committed? That's my first question, in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the instrument is lost, Your Honour, in that the military police, as an organisation, are integrated into the chain of command. And we have been discussing that recently, just a few moments ago. And the investigative steps, as I understand it - and I repeat what you will know already, that I'm not a military lawyer - the investigative steps are relatively straightforward. If there is an incident which might be a disciplinary offence or, indeed, even worse, a crime, then you have your military police on hand, part of this procedure, part of this coordination and collaboration between -- within the chain of command to take the first step in investigating and then handing that on to the military police criminal branch which exists as part of those companies, those battalions. So I'm not sure there is a particular disadvantage. I mean, there might be. But it doesn't seem to me to be -- it seems to be something that can be managed relatively simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Have you also considered that where you said the advantage was that the chain of command might not be happy by certain investigations, that Mr. Lausic might not be -- have been happy with certain investigations either. I mean, whoever is in control of the police may influence the direction in which investigations are conducted. So I would therefore -- because you said it was a well -- careful separation with the advantages. And I'm just asking you whether this could be one of the side effects, that then Mr. Lausic's conduct or those around him would not be investigated.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a Latin phrase which starts "quis custodes" or something like that, which means who looks after the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is a quite straightforward problem, as in any system, who watches those who have the authority to investigate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which would apply both to Mr. Lausic in command, but also the normal chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Yes, my following question is just to avoid that I misunderstand your testimony. You were asked about the focus of an operational commander. You were asked: "What kind of focus and what kind of energy does an operational commander have to bring to bear to accomplish those tasks?" And you said: "Very substantial, physical and mental." And you went back to the idea of prioritisation, and that: "He will wish to ensure that all those things which can be looked after by someone else are looked after by somebody else." I did not -- the whole issue of prioritisation to mean that it would, in any way, relieve himself from his duty to investigate and/or punish if there were any reasons, not that he does it all by himself, but he would still keep that responsibility, even if he was focussing on operational matters.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
