utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I mean, my comments were really on the sort of physical responsibilities in terms of, for example, looking after a garrison. Checking whether the garrison was doing its job. In terms of his responsibilities to military law, he has to ensure -- a commander has to ensure that such things do not get missed because of -- if at all possible. I mean, he must take steps to ensure that there is a proper -- there is a proper organisation who can ensure that those elements are still properly looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think I did not misunderstand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least I'm seeking your confirmation on what I said that seems not to be contradicted by your answer.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then one matter remains, and that is the part of your report dealing with Grubori, which is not a part of your report anymore. I noticed that -- and I'm also, Mr. Cayley, looking in your direction. I notice that some of your findings on Grubori and the responsibility of Mr. Cermak still appear in the report. For example, page 55, you say about General Cermak's role in this affair, being that of a spokesman: "He had no responsibility for the events and lacked authority to influence planning or implementation, even if he had known. He became involved because he was the point of contact." Well, we find your conclusions in this respect in your report -- therefore, I take it that in that paragraph, which is not part of the report anymore, that you have explained on the basis of what you reached these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall my paragraph clearly. I do recall that it was a prece [phoen] of the events which led up to it and a description of what happened. My comments there were really an attempted explanation -- again, Your Honour, right or wrong, I was trying to put a context to General Cermak's actions there. The -- if I remember rightly, there was little -- and you may be surprised at this. There was -- there was little in my workings, my discussion, which actually directly impinged on that conclusion. But my -- my memory is not clear of it because it's some time since I have seen that piece. So I really am -- I would have to go back and look before I could guarantee that my reply was accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may have been little, but you present your conclusions in relation to the role of General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the paragraph being taken out, we do know on what it is exactly based, whether that is little or much. Might even be interested to know, in order to assess the probative value of your conclusions. Mr. Cayley, you will understand I have to discussed with my colleagues -- we understood that, first of all, that we find some of the conclusions in the report not knowing anymore what the basis for it is. That's one. Second, that it was the -- it was not a draft paragraph which was taken out, but it was a fully developed, at least as fully developed as the witness said for a report, not a draft report. He specifically and spontaneously told us that. He even corrected someone who used the words "draft." Under those circumstances and also taking into account that only for practical reasons it was taken out, as we understood, the Chamber wondered whether that paragraph that had been taken out could not be produced, which, of course, could raise another matter, that is whether further questions should be put to the witness about that paragraph. I would like hear your views on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It can be done, Your Honour. I think the witness is indicating that he doesn't have it. We've got that particular paragraph. My suggestion would be to present it to the witness, have him read it and confirm, Yes, this is the paragraph that I wrote. I mean, it's actually more than a paragraph; This is the narrative that I wrote. And then I leave it in the Court's hands after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm also looking at you Mr. Hedaraly. Let's not forget that the Chamber has received quite a bit of evidence on the Grubori incident, and the primary focus apparently from this witness from what I understand is the role of General Cermak and not a reconstruction of responsibilities for the -- but perhaps it is, I do not know. The Chamber is not seeking to go through the whole Grubori evidence again, but the Chamber would like to know, on what the expert witness has based his opinion on these matters which still appear in the report. Now, let's be very practical. Your suggestion is let's give it to Mr. Deverell, that we should invite him to read it. Then the other issue is that Mr. Hedaraly hasn't seen it. And I wouldn't send you both into the same room, Mr. Hedaraly and Mr. Deverell. But an opportunity should be there for the prosecution to review it, also for the other Defence teams to see whether there is anything which triggers any need for further questions. Now, let's then be very practical. It's now a quarter past 4.00. We were scheduled to have a break at ten minutes to 5.00 and then continue at ten minutes past 5.00. Mr. Cayley, how many pages is the Grubori part of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's five pages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does it introduce any sources which are not yet in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Hedaraly, just for a -- they call it a quick-scan nowadays, I think. How much time do you think you would need? And, Mr. Deverell, you may have less problems in going more quickly through what you have written yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that if, for example, you would say 20 minutes would do for the quick-scan or half an hour, or I would consult with my Grubori specialized colleagues -- what I would like to know and find out is how much time we need to come at a point where we would have a sufficient basis to determine how we will further proceed, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think I understand the Chamber to be saying not to gain a full understanding now and decide. But I think to read the five pages and discuss briefly with my colleagues, I think an hour would be reasonable to at least then inform the Chamber as to whether we want to have questions, whether we want to ask questions, whether we want to introduce other documents, look for documents. We may not have any questions for the witness. I think an hour to provide that initial information and able to consult would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- with regard to the Grubori matter, I was just talking about questions that I have based on Your Honours' questions. I have a few questions based on the questions, Mr. President, that you asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just wanted to put that on the record that in the mix of time, I just ask the Court's leave to ask some follow-up questions to General Deverell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you do that before you had seen the relevant portion of the report on Grubori or, rather, look at that first and then see whether you have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I could look at the report and see if I have any additional questions, or I could ask the questions that I have now. Anything Your Honours would like to do, I'm ready to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has not asked yet, Mr. Kuzmanovic, how much time he would need to read the five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know need an hour, Judge, but I would like to look at it. I have not seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. We give you, Mr. Hedaraly, until 5.00 to form a provisional opinion on how to proceed, and if that would be to put further questions to the witness, to put those, unless good cause is shown that you couldn't do it right away and that would you need further investigations. That's the reason why I asked Mr. Cayley whether there is any new evidentiary material on which the expert witness forms his opinion. Since the Chamber is seeking this, we would like to receive a copy as well, so I take it that we will find a way to copy these five pages for every interested party and for the bench. Then if we resume at 5.00, under normal circumstances we would finish at not later than 6.30. Just for the parties to know, there are a few matters which are still outstanding, some pending issues in which the Chamber is seeking further information from the parties. If any time remains after we've dealt with the Grubori, the Chamber would like to put those matters -- to raise those matters with the parties. The Chamber further would like to deal with the MFI list, most likely the second half of tomorrow morning. For those purposes a list will be given to the parties, provisional list of what MFIs are still outstanding, so that the parties have at least some time and I will have some time as well to prepare for a housekeeping session later tomorrow morning. I'm thinking at this moment in terms of 11.00 or 11.30. We'll first have this break, and having read the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just interrupt and ask your permission to give a copy to General Deverell, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we -- I think I followed your suggestion. Mr. Kehoe, the questions you had in mind, the Chamber suggests that you keep them until you have read the report and then put them all at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll have a break until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have read the relevant portion which was once part of the report. I'd first like to briefly inquire into whether -- we said we'd like to see it, and we wanted to know what was the basis on which the witness had based his opinion, an opinion which does appear on other parts of the report. But the first question is whether anyone would like to have this in evidence. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be obviously conditional on a proper opportunity to cross-examine this witness. And based on what you stated earlier that unless good cause is shown, that would have to be done immediately. We are not in a position to begin cross-examination on this portion at this stage. So if it is conditional on us beginning our cross-examination now, then we would prefer that it not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cayley, I know that you were not the one who -- who moved this. It was the Chamber curious about the basis that triggered all this. What would be your position at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think we would reserve or position depending on what the Prosecution are going to do now, in essence. And how they're going to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had a chance to review this. My position is under 94 bis, we should have had this report obviously within -- we had 30 days within which to object or to find out whether we're going cross-examine this witness, which we did. We advised the Chamber that we would cross-examine the witness. This part was not in the initial report. Obviously just got it now. I read it. I'd have some substantial issues to deal with in cross-examination if the report is admitted. My simple solution is I would -- my suggestion is not to admit this and to remove the conclusion or exclude the conclusions on Grubori in the report that General Sir Jack Deverell made, and that would probably be an equitable way to deal with this issue, but otherwise, I would have some significant cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no position on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the things the Chamber considered is the following: First of all, in this document, which once was part of the report, we find a lot of references to matters that are in evidence. In addition to that, and, for example, I'm referring to the middle of the third page. We find, not for the first time, the view of the -- the opinion of the expert on -- on the position of General Cermak. That's not exclusively here. That, to some extent, repeats what we find elsewhere in the report as well. A new element is that the expert witness has visited Grubori village. That is -- of course, that adds to what many of the other witnesses could tell us. Some of them have visited the village or the area; many have not. As far as the conclusions are concerned, the Chamber provisionally formed an opinion that, in many respects, the opinions are not really within the field of expertise of this witness. Mr. Deverell, if I would use the word amateur psychology here and there, you would certainly forgive me for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour. I would. I read it, and I accept the point you make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes you put on paper what you believe; sometimes you come to conclusions that it seems most likely that there was an armed man discovered in the hamlet and that the civilians were killed either by accident, but more probably in the retribution for giving him sanctuary. That is all -- well, the basis for that from the facts, the evidentiary basis we've seen is not fully transparent, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber suggests that we would not receive, among other matters, for at least one of the reasons that we would not receive this document as part of the report in evidence, and that -- and the Chamber would like to know whether the Cermak Defence is willing to strike the now unfounded opinions of the witness about the Grubori in the role of General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I discussed the matter with Mr. Kay, and he agrees with the Chamber that it doesn't actually take us anywhere, this. And in fact that is one of the original reasons he advised that it shouldn't be part of the main report for the reasons you've said, Your Honour. So we are quite happy to strike the conclusion and for this not to go into evidence. We agree with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I look at the other parties to see whether they could live with such a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We could live with it, Mr. President. And just for my own reference, we're talking page 55 of the report, lines 17 to 26. I think those are the only parts dealing with the matter. If I'm mistaken, either General Deverell or my learned friend, Mr. Cayley, can indicate if there's any other portions where Grubori is discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one I spotted earlier. Is that -- and, of course, I have not read the report specifically in view of that, and I haven't checked any footnotes, but at least there seems to be agreement that that is the part where clearly Grubori --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There's no other part, Your Honour. It's -- the wording, I think Mr. Hedaraly checked -- I, sorry, am checking to see whether the wording is the same, the conclusion in the extract and in the report, so that part can be stricken that he has indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'm looking at you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am grateful that the Chamber has accepted my proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, any questions in relation to which is now not even be a part of the report anymore, that is -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: None on the Grubori issue, Mr. President, just on your questions, Mr. President, prior to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although I think they were mainly about -- oh, yes -- you mean entirely apart from the Grubori incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, I may have misunderstood you at an earlier stage for which I then apologise. You have an opportunity to put further questions. Yes, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just when we say stricken, I'm just wondering logistically if there will be, as we have done before, a new version of the report with that paragraph redacted that will be uploaded, or whether it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we'll find ways to make this effective, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Because if you recall, Your Honour, it is only marked for identification because of the issue of the page numbering. So we can actually upload a new version and show it to Mr. Hedaraly, and I think we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that before the judgement, we will have to find a version [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yeah, you will. You will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be appreciated, Mr. Cayley. Then, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I hope this is the last time I'm questioning here, but I do have a few follow-up questions based on your colloquy with the President. And it had to do with the comment that you made as who watches the people doing the investigations. And -- and in the circumstances of the HV, there was in fact a security and information service attached to the Split Military District that was in fact there to monitor whether the military police were doing their job. Was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would take your word for it. I'm not entirely certain of the exact role of -- of the SIS. But my comment -- my comment was really specifically on -- based on the principle of the separation of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, my question was also not about the factual, but about my understanding of advantages and disadvantages of a certain system. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just within the system, do you know that there was a SIS element, Security and Information Service element, attached to the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think did I. Yes, I would have -- I recognised you -- that you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me change subjects if we may and just touch on the questions that Judge Orie asked about the operational commander issues. And I harken back to your testimony yesterday at page 24200 when you and I were discussing what an operational commander is doing in the circumstances where is he planning for and conducting military operation. And you noted in line 12, on page 24200: "My experience is that once you actually confront the reality, then you're planning activity becoming more frenetic and more demanding. So the commander is absolutely focussed and he doesn't have time to deal with other matters and has to prioritise very profoundly at times on what he is to concentrate on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I consulted with my colleagues. The only thing I did is to verify whether I understood the answer of the witness correctly. Therefore, now going again in factual matters which were not in any way raised by me is not what the Chamber expects to you do at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- on that score, I would like to explore the answer that the witness gave to your question, Mr. President, on page 92 today, from line 17 to 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were talking about the obligations of an operational commander, starting, if we can, just on line 19: "In terms of his responsibilities to military law, he has to ensure, a commander has to ensure that such things do not get missed, if at all possible. I mean, he must take steps to ensure there is a proper -- there a proper organisation who can ensure that those elements are still properly looked after." So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kehoe, I asked the witness whether I had understood his answer well. He gave some explanations. So I -- apart from verifying whether I had understood something not to be part of his answer, he then briefly explains that I had understood it. I verified it with him. One or two questions, fine. But we're not going to go into the whole area again. Again, the main issue was whether I had well understood that what he said was not touching upon the responsibility of a commander. That's what I asked. That's what the witness answered. And that's what I raised, and that's -- if that triggers any question, you may proceed. But let's keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just consult with you, Mr. President. Because I will just go to the area of inquiry and if Your Honours want to have that question, then I will ask. If not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said, you may proceed, but it's -- I take it that it's clear to you that the Chamber considers the matter that was raised of a limited nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what I would like to explore with you, General, is the comment that you have, that the -- a proper organisation who can ensure those elements are still properly looked after. Or looked at, excuse me. And if we can -- and I want to ask you just elaborating on this, if this is the type of situation that you are referring to, and this is a transcript of the tape of the video on the 6th of August that you viewed. And this is at transcript page [sic] D979. And that's -- excuse me, page 4 in the English. Exhibit D979, page 4 in the English. We can start with that paragraph: "We are faced ..." towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe, again, for your guidance, I did not raise the issue whether General Gotovina fulfilled any duty. My question was limited to whether I would have to understand the answer of the witness as relieving a commander from his duty. I wasn't even talking about General Gotovina. It was in general terms. We're talking about a commanding -- operational commander. I did not raise the issue whether or not an operational commander, in the person of General Gotovina, met that obligation, yes or no. That was not a matter which was raised by me, and I want you to keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to get crosswise with the Chamber. Obviously the only operational commander specifically in the courtroom is General Gotovina. So I thought that's what we were discussing. And the only thing that I was talking about was just this setting up of a proper support organisation to take care of those elements and then pointing the witness to the elements that General Gotovina talks about in the 6th August 1995 meeting at the -- at the castle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then to ask him what, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To see if those are the types of organisations and elements that would you expect an operational commander to have established in order to ensure that any ill-conduct or any wrongful conduct is looked at and curtailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber's ruling is, Mr. Kehoe, that I did not raise any factual matter in this respect and that therefore the Chamber, at this moment, expects you not to revisit the factual basis for an answer to the question, whether or not General Gotovina met any obligation in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I will be guided by your ruling. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, it's been a pleasure. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I had one question from Mr. Kehoe's previous re-direct examination. I did not want to -- don't know what the proper procedural order was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that Mr. Kehoe cross-examined the witness, so he did not conduct any re-direct examination. This, of course, creates all of the problems all of the times, because part of cross-examination could be to raise any matter the witness may have knowledge about and which may -- may support the case of that cross-examining party. I will very carefully listen to your question whether it is appropriate or not to put it, but you may formulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have D1006 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, General, you will see that's the order for inspection that Mr. Kehoe showed to you. And I believe it was the last page. And there was a suggestion put to you that one of the possible reasons why this Knin garrison was not listed was because of the special relationship between General Cermak and General Gotovina. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, you will note that this order also is not sent to the Vrgorac garrison, the Imotski garrison, and the Dubrovnik garrison. And my question for you is in your review of all of the documents that have, have you come across anything that suggested a special relationship between the commander of those garrisons and General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I interrupt, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is there some foundation that those garrisons are part of the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: D33 and P2656, D33 and P2656. P2656 being the document we saw yesterday about cancelling the commands of certain garrisons. And there was a list of garrisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We also can be very practical, Mr. Kehoe, that if they are outside the scope, then that explains everything anyhow. So therefore let's see whether the witness can answer the question, if would --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. We can go into it. I can go through the documentation because there was some changes within the Split Military District at different time-frames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do not have the details on the top of my head at this moment. Mr. Hedaraly, you have asked the witness whether there was any such special relationship of the commanders of those garrisons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I saw no evidence to lead me to suppose there was a special relationship between the commanders of those garrisons and the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I'm looking through the courtroom. This concludes your evidence, Mr. Deverell. I'd like to thank you very much - usually say for coming to The Hague. But in your case, I should say coming two times today, which is even more than most witness do. I would like to thank you for having answered all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Deverell out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have some time left I would like to deal with a few procedural matters and leave the MFI list for tomorrow. I do understand that the parties have received an updated MFI list. Mr. Misetic, I'm addressing you. There is still this motion to enforce the Trial Chamber's previous Rule 54 bis order that's in relation to Brussels, to say so. Now we know that you travelled to Brussels, and we -- you more or less promised us that you would provide us with a list of still sort documents. We do know that you refer to some of them as very important, but as far as the Chamber is aware of, we never received that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There is one document in particular that we're looking for, and so to that extent, I did -- I have followed up and intended to file that with the Chamber. But I think the Chamber has been made aware of what document that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you mentioned that on the 25th August if I am correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the RC Knin log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the only one you, at this moment, would you want the Chamber to take further action on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Then the list is rather short. But that is clear. Then for the information of the parties, the Chamber will consider on short notice whether we'll seek further explanation or not from CLSS in relation to the translation of D970; that is, the fire or the strikes translation, two documents where we had different translations and where you had already submitted it to CLSS, Mr. Misetic. You -- then one of the translations of the word, I think it was "udara," was then changed. You asked for an explanation and that explanation was given at the time as being the best one or the good one. The Chamber will consider whether we will seek any further explanation from CLSS. We are still considering that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think from our perspective the critical issue is that the word be translated the same in the two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, as a matter of fact that in response to you, that they had chosen for -- but I would have to check that then on my ... I'm afraid I don't have it here, although I recently saw it. I think there was -- that a choice was made, but let me just check for one second. I think I have it, but I have it on my computer rather than anywhere else. If I would summarise what appears on the transcript, is that the Gotovina Defence asked CLSS for a check and that CLSS gave a new translation of D970, translating "udara" as fire. That it is the Gotovina Defence position that the proper translation should be strikes, as it was used in P1272. And that you had asked for an explanation and that the response by CLSS was that the essence of the translation is accurate. I'm now just summarizing very briefly my information. And is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is my understanding as well, Mr. President, but I confess I must check. And if I could get back to you tomorrow morning on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider the matter further, but we might wait until we have heard from you tomorrow morning before we would take any action, if we would, in the direction of CLSS. Yes. Then I move to my next item. Yes, the next item is Cermak's motion for admission of witnesses from Milosevic and Martic under Rule 92 bis, and there is a related matter, the motion for the admission of evidence pursuant to 92 quater, and there is a disclosure issue. Mr. Kay, last time we were informed that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can tell Your Honour that the final typographic errors have been done so that is ready now as a document to go before the Trial Chamber and deal with that part of the disclosure issue, if I can put it that way, concerning the -- the evidence that goes to the Rule 68 issues that the Trial Chamber decided upon. The outstanding disclosure of the Rule 68 issues has still to be dealt with, and I flagged this up with the Trial Chamber a couple of weeks ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The 5th of November, I think, was the last time where Ms. Higgins explained to us what was dealt with and that the disclosure issue was still not settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In the sense that we know what we're talking about and the Trial Chamber ruled upon it, but we have not had the information yet that needs to be disclosed and then managed in a way that is appropriate to the evidence, without overburdening the process. There are four to six, I'm informed. Really it comes down to this, Your Honour. I have looked at this material. And it's striking we've had nothing from Civljane, Cetina, Kijevo, Drnis, all these places we know about. And we know that there is stuff there that has not surfaced in the disclosure process. And in these circumstances we have had so far 250 documents in 13 batches or so. Numbers don't help. It's the information that -- that we want. I know it's there because I was involved in another case some years ago where these areas were known about me when I came to this case, and that's only there had been a disclosure of it. That still has to be dealt with. I don't think that this is an issue that prevents closure of the case, because what we're effectively talking about is the paper acceptance of evidence by the Court, the documentary form of evidence rather than viva voce or witness evidence. We are essentially talking about evidence that finds its way to the Trial Chamber in sufficient time for people to deal with it in their final briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, I appreciate your observations. At the same time, we are looking at it at this moment for housekeeping purposes primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do understand that it needs intensified attention to settle this matter at this moment. And it really is important that the -- that clarity is achieved as quickly as possible from our -- Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are trying very hard. I think the Chamber can appreciate the volume of material that is needed to be reviewed. As my learned friend had said, 13 batches have already been produced. There are four to six outstanding, and we are going municipality by municipality, so perhaps that the reasons that the ones that Mr. Kay now says are missing are still not there. That being said, we are doing our best and we are working very hard behind the scenes to get all this material to the Cermak Defence pursuant to the Court's order. On the related matter of the motion for admission, that is almost ready to be submitted. And that is correct. As well, there are a few qualifications that the Prosecution would like to make, and those have been agreed and discussed with the Cermak Defence. So hopefully we will be able to finalize this very shortly, and it shouldn't be something that, I think, would take an unreasonably long amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have the disclosure issue, we have the 92 bis admission of witnesses from the Milosevic and the Martic case. Now there is also, and seems to be related, the Cermak's motion for the admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 quater. Is that related, and is that settled already or ... We -- I do remember that the Gotovina Defence did not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's in the schedule, Your Honour. That's something that we've dealt it. I think we have managed all this material into the single document which is the way we're going forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine. That's -- I just wanted to verify that it being a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a distinct motion to see whether this was covered by what has been achieved until now as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're a little bit disjointed on it because we have been heavily struck down by illness in the last two weeks, and the back room people who have been looking at this have been unavailable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I move to the submission of two Rule 92 ter statement, the one witness IC-32; the other one, IC-24. These witness will not be called from what I understand. Could I seek confirmation that the -- that they will not be called, and that therefore that the 92 ter -- the submission of the 92 ter statements is withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have called our witnesses now. General Sir Jack Deverell was the last one, Your Honour. The outstanding matter is the 92 bis and other documentary-type evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we knew already that witnesses IC-1 and IC-2 would not be called, but may I then take it that also the submission their 92 ter statements are also withdrawn at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. That is implicit, Your Honour, in our announcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it should be on the record somewhere. That's the reason why I raised the matter. Then I have one other matter. On 9 October of this year, for transparency reasons, the parties were invited to the review the record and submit no later than the 6th of November a list of bar table submissions in this case and attach any informally communicated spreadsheets in order to appropriately put certain matters on the record. The Chamber has not received such a filing, and, therefore, I would like to inquire with the parties whether this silence means that they consider the record appropriately be transparent in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if -- on behalf of the Prosecution I can go first while my learned friends consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still working, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: On the Prosecution side, it turned out that what we thought was going to be initially a very simple task turned out to be little more complicated because it involved a lot of e-mail communications back and forth with the Defence teams, not necessarily just spreadsheets but also in the context of exhibits saying we'll bar table this document, we'll bar table that one, and there was not always a formal discussion or objection. So going through all the e-mails of 18 months or more of trial turned out to be a task that was more onerous than we had thought initially. So if we could ask the Court until next weeks to provide that, we are working on it, and we will try to have it by then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber was actually informed about -- by Mr. Waespi, at least the Chamber staff was informed, that the joint filing we asked for, that it would take some more time. But the Chamber would like to know how much more. And I fully understand that the matter turns out to be more complex than it looked at at first instance, but we'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Out of a abundance of caution, if I say Friday of next week, then I think that should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we expect not later than -- let me see. Yes, we expect not later than Friday next week, the joint submission by the parties. Yes. The next issue is the following. The Chamber staff went through the MFI list, and it appears - I usually refrain from looking at it too early - but it appears that there are 16 MFIs on that list. Now we could schedule a hearing tomorrow which would perhaps good for the Markac Defence so that they could start their case with a clean slate on Monday morning. At the same time, it also takes your time, Mr. Kuzmanovic, tomorrow. We would have to schedule a session for that purpose only. I would like to hear from you whether would you prefer to have a bit contaminated the start of your case by first dealing with MFI lists, which is not perhaps the thing you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honor, it really doesn't matter to us. I think if the MFI list is short. I noticed that there are no exhibits that relate to our defence on the MFI list. I don't have a problem if we start that on Monday and get it done with. And start -- and have the rest of the week free. But we're more than willing and able to participate tomorrow for a short session if Court wishes to do so and get that done with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would like to hear from the other parties whether they would prefer not to have a session tomorrow and deal with the MFIs on Monday or whether they would prefer to have this from the table before we start hearing the Markac case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for our part we've only got two documents, one of which is General Sir Jack Deverell's report which is being dealt with, so that's a matter. And the other one was just a document that has a translation already uploaded and is already linked. So the rest concerns my learned friends for Mr. Gotovina's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic or Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we meet tomorrow, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we going meet tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, we can meet Monday morning; it's fine. If Your Honour wants to meet tomorrow, I know that my client would prefer not to be here for an MFI session. And I suspect that -- I don't want to speak for the other gentlemen, but I suspect they don't want to come either. With that being said, Monday is fine, and we will be guided by Your Honours' wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, we certainly would not want to be the only ones to cause a hearing tomorrow, so we will postpone till Monday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decided that there's no need to have a special hearing tomorrow for MFI, although the accused would have been allowed not to be present. But it's perhaps also for counsel not the thing you're looking forward to, to come back to this Tribunal. So, therefore, we'll deal with the MFIs on Monday. Is there any other matter to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Monday is a witness scheduled for the Markac Defence as well as this administrative matters, which the Cermak Defence have no great interest in. Mr. Cermak has had a pressing request for a personal visit on that day. I've discussed the matter with him this afternoon. And with the Court's leave we ask that he not be present for the hearing on Monday. The evidence does not concern him and it's not intended to concern him in relation to that witness, and his interests will be covered by counsel, with the Court's approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber accepts that Mr. Cermak prefers not to be present, which means that he does not exercises his right to be present for this one morning hearing, his right to be present --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at trial. And since he is always there, it meets no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And he is extremely grateful for that, as well as the reason for the visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other matter to be raised? If not, I established that apart from the housekeeping matters that this concludes the presentation of the Cermak Defence case apart from decisions still to be taken on admission of the report and some minor matters, but as far as witnesses are concerned ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Effectively closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, therefore, the presentation of the Cermak case is closed. We will adjourn, and we will resume on Monday, the 16th of November, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.54 p.m.,
